chapters.title: Chapter 1051. The One Point His Calculations Couldn’t Account For
paragraphs: She emerged from the twisted skeleton of the Nightwing household just as Theo’s attention was fractured by Apollo’s work below.

She didn’t stumble out from under debris or rush out in a panic; she moved with the measured, relentless momentum of someone who had been holding back a flood within the walls while the world collapsed outside.

She had spent the last several minutes managing the internal chaos, triage, and containment, the brutal reality of holding people together while their bones snapped under shifting foundations, and now she was emerging to assess the external catastrophe.
Her eyes, sharp and unblinking, performed a rapid tactical sweep.

She cataloged the devastation: the cratered street where civilians lay convulsing; the jagged breach in the Academy’s outer wall that looked like a wound torn in flesh; the hairline fractures spiderwebbing across the Nightwing estate’s foundation; and finally, the residual shiver of the temporal distortion field still clinging to the air like radioactive dust.
Then, her gaze climbed upward. She found him.
Theo hung suspended in the air, a broken monument to power without control. When his eyes met hers, the reaction was instantaneous and visceral.
The amber aura surrounding him didn’t brighten with hope or dim with shame; it underwent a violent, turbulent shift.
It became unstable, the energy flickering with the erratic frequency of a heart arrhythmia, the unmistakable signature of an emotional state that had been violently overridden by an unexpected input.
"Theo," Aurelia said.
The name didn’t carry the authority of a matriarch, the discipline of a combat instructor, or the practiced neutrality of a political figure. It was something far more dangerous.

It was the voice she had used in those quiet, fragile hours of his childhood, the voice of a mother who had spent years trying to navigate the impossible terrain of raising a child who was born to be a storm.

Rex watched, his mind racing, analyzing the shift. His emotional insight and soul manipulation systems tools, designed to read the deepest currents of human intent, suddenly spiked with error messages.
They had predicted resistance, anger, or guilt. They had not predicted this.
Theo’s expression had been a fortress. For years, he had been building it, layer by layer, until he was nothing but a closed system of controlled trauma and divine detachment.
But as Aurelia spoke, something unprecedented happened. The fortress didn’t crumble; it simply opened.
It was a microscopic breach at the one point Rex’s calculations couldn’t fully account for: the raw, primal hinge of the mother-son bond.

It was that involuntary crack in the armor that occurs in the split second before a man decides whether to break down or stand tall. For one heartbeat, the god disappeared, and only the exhausted boy remained.
"You look terrible," Aurelia said.
Her tone was almost conversational, cutting through the apocalyptic tension of the morning with a devastating normalcy.
Theo’s throat worked visibly.
"I know," he rasped, his voice cracking like dry earth.
"You are bleeding from your eye," she said.
Her eyes traced the crimson trail that had dried across his cheekbone, the blood seeping from a tear in his socket where the pressure of his own power had literally ruptured the capillaries.
"I know," he said again.
The admission was hollow, stripped of all pretense.
"Come down," she commanded, though it sounded less like an order and more like an invitation to stop pretending. "Not because I am telling you to."
"Not because I am your superior. But because standing up there bleeding and staring at nothing is not doing anything productive."
Theo didn’t look at Aurelia first. His gaze snapped sideways, sharp as a blade, landing on Rex. His eyes were bloodshot, pupils blown wide with adrenaline and something far more corrosive.
He was searching Rex’s face for something—a confession, a smirk, a sign of triumph—but Rex offered nothing but a terrifying, analytical stillness.
Rex didn’t blink. He didn’t acknowledge the accusation in Theo’s eyes.

He simply calculated the distance between Theo’s suspended form and the cracked asphalt below, measuring the potential energy of a fall that would be catastrophic if the temporal enhancement failed mid-descent.
He said nothing, his silence a wall of cold marble.

"Theo," Aurelia said, her voice cutting through the static. "Whatever you believe Rex is or has done, whatever the god that gave that power told you, and whatever you felt at that cliff, you are still my child."
"And my child is standing forty meters above a street bleeding from his eye, and I am asking him to come down."
The wind howled between them, carrying the metallic tang of blood and the burnt ozone smell of spent energy. Theo’s jaw clenched so hard the muscle spasmed visibly.
His voice came out in a low murmur, a sound that shouldn’t have carried thirty meters, yet Rex caught it with perfect clarity:
"He took everything."
"I know," Aurelia replied.
There was no denial in her voice. No defensive lie could soften the blow.
She met his accusation with the brutal honesty of someone who had already mourned what was lost. "Come down."
"He took you," Theo spat, the words dripping with a raw, childlike betrayal that made the godlike power surrounding him seem like a grotesque costume.
Aurelia went silent. For several seconds, the only sound was the distant scream of a siren and the wet coughing of civilians trying to remember how to breathe.
The air between them felt pressurized, as if the universe itself were holding its breath, waiting to see if the boy would break or the mother would bend.
"Theo," she said finally, her voice steadier than steel. "Come down."
The amber-gold corona around him shuddered. It wasn’t a sudden collapse or a dramatic surrender.

It was something more profound: the soundless surrender of a dam that had finally stopped fighting the water. The effort required to maintain the temporal field, the sheer cognitive and biological tax of holding reality apart, was suddenly withdrawn.
The aura didn’t explode; it simply bled away, dissipating from the radius in a slow, exhausted exhale. The field wasn’t defeated; it was simply abandoned.
As the energy faded, the world snapped back into focus.

The buildings’ stone walls, which had been flickering and phasing between temporal states like bad film stock, solidified with an audible groan of settling masonry. The air lost its nauseating shiver, returning to standard physical parameters.

At the field’s edge, the people who had been convulsing in temporal loops began the painful, graceless process of biological recovery, gasping for air and vomiting from disorientation, their bodies slowly reacquainting themselves with the linear flow of time.
Then came the descent.
Theo didn’t float down like a god; he fell like a man. His temporal enhancements were still functioning at a residual level, preventing a terminal impact, but his body was spent.
The muscles in his legs were twitching from overexertion, and his breathing was ragged. He hit the pavement with a bone-jarring thud, the impact sending a spiderweb of cracks through the street.
He stayed down for a heartbeat, hands pressed against the asphalt, head hanging low. Blood dripped from his eye socket, pattering onto the concrete with rhythmic, wet sounds.
Then, he forced himself upright. His legs shook, but he stood. He looked at Aurelia with the hollow stare of someone who had seen the end of the world and found it wanting.
Aurelia didn’t hesitate. She crossed the distance between them, stepping over debris and bloodstained rubble without breaking stride.

When she reached him, she performed the singular, instinctive ritual of a mother who has seen her child reduced to broken fragments: she reached up and cupped his face. Her palm pressed against the uninjured side of his cheek, her thumb brushing just below his temple.

She didn’t coddle him; she searched him. Her eyes moved over his features with a flat, clinical assessment, checking the bone structure, the pupil response, and the reality of his presence, ensuring that the person standing before her was still the son she knew, despite the carnage.
"I am still angry with you," Theo said. His voice was hoarse, stripped of its divine timbre.
"I know," she said.
"That does not go away because you came out," he challenged, his voice cracking with the remnants of his fury.
"I know," Aurelia said, her grip on his face tightening just enough to ground him. "Come inside..."
"Let someone look at your eye."

chapters.title: Chapter 1052. I Chose the Path of Guaranteed Adaptation Over Uncertain Heroism
paragraphs: Theo turned his head one last time. His gaze didn’t just land on Rex; it pierced through him, fueled by a hatred so concentrated it felt like a physical pressure in the air between them.
Through the haze of pain and the blood streaming from his ruptured eye, Theo saw through the mask of the perfect assistant. He saw the architect of the catastrophe.

He saw the cold, calculating monster that had orchestrated every moment of this breakdown. He knew exactly that Rex was a predator wearing the skin of a protector, and he knew that every word Rex had spoken, every ’logical’ assessment, had been a calculated move in a game. Theo was only now beginning to understand.
Rex met that stare with terrifying neutrality. His pupils didn’t dilate; his breathing didn’t quicken.
He looked at Theo not as an enemy but as a specimen under glass.
Something passed between them in that silence, a wordless, venomous acknowledgment. It wasn’t a truce, and it certainly wasn’t a resolution.

It was the grim recognition that this engagement had reached a temporary stalemate, a point where continuing would require both of them to expend something they couldn’t afford: more violence, more exposure, more truth.
Neither of them was going to blink. Neither of them was going to give the other the satisfaction of a concession.
Rex was the first to break the contact. He averted his eyes with a clinical precision that felt more insulting than a physical blow.
He didn’t look away because he was cowed; he looked away because his calculations had shifted. His mind was already moving toward the next phase of the operation: the next twenty minutes.

For the plan to succeed, Aurelia needed to successfully steer this broken, volatile asset Theo into the controlled environment of the household’s interior before the window of his current vulnerability closed.
If Theo collapsed now, or worse, if his rage triggered another uncontrolled discharge, the entire sequence would fail.
Behind the impenetrable calm of his expression, behind the mask of the flawless innocent man he’s playing, Rex felt something else. A cold, dark satisfaction.
A private, silent laugh echoed in the deepest recesses of his consciousness. ’Hook, line, and sinker.’
Theo had reacted exactly as predicted. The trauma, the betrayal, the collapse—it was all part of the design.
He had fallen directly into the trap, driven there by the very emotions Rex had so carefully manipulated.
"Theo," Aurelia said, her voice breaking through his spiraling fury like a lifeline. "Move. Now."
She didn’t wait for his consent. She placed her hand on his shoulder not as a gesture of comfort, but as a physical anchor, a command disguised as support.
She began to steer him toward the courtyard gate, her body positioned to shield him from Rex’s sight.
Theo moved. But he didn’t move like a warrior or a god.

He moved with the hollow, mechanical quality of a man who had burned his entire soul to ash and was now operating on nothing but muscle memory and the singular, desperate need to obey the one person who still saw him as human.

Every step was a struggle against gravity and exhaustion; his boots dragged across the debris, leaving crimson smears where his blood dripped onto the cracked pavement. His shoulder slumped under Aurelia’s touch, his entire posture screaming of a profound, spiritual defeat.

Rex stood motionless in the center of the devastation, a solitary figure amidst the ruins. He watched them retreat, the mother carrying the broken son back into the fortress, his eyes tracking their movement with the detached interest of a chess player watching a pawn move toward its inevitable sacrifice.
Rex turned his head slowly. His gaze found Morwenna, who stood at the ragged edge of the street like a sentinel carved from ancient stone.

She wasn’t panicked; she was something far more dangerous: she was processing. Her eyes swept over the carnage, the twitching bodies, the cracked foundations, and the blood-slicked asphalt, and then she fixed her attention on him with the terrifying focus of a predator assessing a new threat.
"Inside," Rex said.
His voice was terrifyingly calm, devoid of the tremor that should accompany witnessing a massacre. "Both of them need someone who is not me."
Morwenna didn’t blink. She met his stare with the flat, glacial assessment of a woman who had spent forty years mastering the art of reading souls and seeing through lies.
She didn’t see an assistant; she saw a surgeon who had let the patient bleed out to study the arterial spray.
"You," she said, the word carrying the weight of a death sentence, "could have stopped this earlier."
"I stopped it when it needed stopping," Rex replied.
His tone was conversational, almost bored, as if they were discussing weather patterns rather than the psychological and physical evisceration of a young man.
"You could have stopped it before the children were affected," she snapped, her voice dropping to a dangerous register. "Before Theo was broken."
Rex looked at her. For a fraction of a second, something flickered behind his eyes—not guilt, not remorse, but something darker: the cold satisfaction of a predator watching a trap spring.
"Yes," he said. "I could have."
"But the adaptation required full expression contact to cover the area distortion’s mechanism. Full expression contact required the field to reach its operational parameters."

Morwenna turned her head toward the field’s outer radius. In the distance, Apollo was moving through the crowd, his hands stained with blood as he knelt beside civilians whose bones had been twisted into impossible angles by the temporal fluctuations.
The screams were fading into low, wet moans of agony.
"You used them," Morwenna said.
It wasn’t a question. It was an accusation that stripped away every pretense of his helpfulness.
"You used Theo’s trauma as a test subject. You used these people as collateral for your own data."
Rex’s expression remained impassive. Inside his mind, his processors hummed with cold efficiency.
’Emotional variables: Morwenna has high hostility.’
’Logic parameters: Defensive deflection.’
’Objective: Maintain plausible deniability while framing casualties as statistical inevitabilities.’

"The adaptation’s coverage prevents the mechanism from reaching anyone I am actively protecting in future applications," Rex said, his words precise as a scalpel. "The first contact requirement is the cost of the coverage."
"I chose to absorb that cost myself rather than prevent the expression."

"But the field reached the civilians anyway," Morwenna challenged, stepping closer. "The people screaming in the street, the children whose minds have been fractured—they were not part of your ’cost,’ Rex."

"The field’s area expression," Rex countered, stepping into her space with a calm that was more threatening than rage, "was going to reach its radius regardless of what I did with the first contact requirement."
"Theo deployed it at scale. The radius was set by the designation’s current power level, not by my choices."

"My choice was whether to prevent the mechanism from reaching me specifically, which would not have affected the field’s radius or its secondary effects on anyone outside my direct protective coverage."
The implication was venomous: ’I saved myself. The rest was irrelevant.’
Morwenna’s eyes narrowed. "You could have contained the field."
"The Earthen Authority that you received from Tremor includes the geological work you have been developing for months."
"You could have anchored the reality around them. You could have—"

"I could have attempted it," Rex interrupted, his voice cutting through her anger like ice through flesh. "Attempting geological containment of a divine temporal working at first application against a mechanism I had not yet adapted to would have had a success probability I was not willing to stake the outcome on."

He paused, letting the cold logic hang between them, a shield of rationality that made her moral outrage seem hysterical. "I chose the path of guaranteed adaptation over the path of uncertain heroism."
"In any other equation, Morwenna, that is called being correct."

His voice dropped an octave, losing its synthetic politeness. "The question isn’t whether they were included."
"The question is whether their value outweighed the data gained from their suffering."
"In this instance, the answer was a resounding yes."
He watched her carefully. He could see the way her shoulders trembled, not from fear, but from the sheer weight of the truth he had laid bare.
He felt a surge of dark, possessive triumph. He didn’t just want to defeat her; he wanted to dismantle her.

He wanted to watch the light of her principles burn out until there was nothing left but a hollow shell, a creature that would eventually crawl to his feet, broken and begging, to serve his every whim, whether that be as a tool, a puppet, or a plaything.

He could already envision it: the proud Morwenna reduced to a trembling slave, her dignity traded for the scraps of survival he would deign to grant her. It was all a matter of time. The pieces were already moving.
Morwenna turned away from him. Her expression was the specific, haunted mask of someone who had asked for the truth and received a monster in return.
She looked like someone who had just realized they were standing in the middle of a minefield and every step forward was a gamble with annihilation.

She began to walk toward the courtyard gate, her movements stiff, each step seeming to cost her more effort than the last. She stopped at the threshold, the ancient stone archway framing her broken silhouette.
"Rex Rexilion," she said.
She didn’t turn around. She spoke to the air, to the ruins, to the god of this new, shattered reality.
"Yes," he said.
"You are exactly as dangerous as Theo said you were," she whispered. "You aren’t a protector. You’re a plague."
Then she went inside, leaving him alone in the wreckage.
Rex stood alone in the center of the devastation. Above him, the massive wall of the Nightwing household hung like a broken jaw, jagged stone teeth exposed to the sky.

In the middle distance, the Academy wall groaned, its structural integrity compromised. Through the haze of dust and blood, he could still see Apollo moving among the wounded, a solitary figure performing the grim work of stitching reality back together, one broken body at a time.
Rex felt nothing but a flat, crystalline satisfaction.
The engagement had been a perfect success. The variables had aligned with mathematical precision.

He had extracted the full temporal designation’s capability profile from the combat engagement. He had witnessed the raw data of Apollo’s life affinity as it fought to reassert biological order over temporal chaos.
He had successfully forced Aurelia and Theo into the household together, the exact configuration required for the next phase of his psychological conditioning.
And most importantly, he had secured Morwenna’s confirmation of his nature, delivered at the exact moment when the others were too distracted by their own pain to hear it.
He stood in the middle of the carnage and took a slow, measured breath. The air tasted of copper and burnt energy, the perfume of victory.
Then, he turned his back on the screaming and the blood. He began to walk toward the academy’s interior gate.
There was administrative work to be done, reports to file, damage assessments to authorize, and resources to reallocate. After all, administrative work did not pause for satisfaction.
The interior of the Nightwing household was suffocating. The air was thick with the smell of antiseptic, old wood, and the iron tang of blood that seemed to have seeped into the very floorboards.
The door had barely clicked shut behind them before the dam broke.

Theo didn’t just explode; he detonated. A guttural, animalistic roar ripped from his throat as he hurled himself against the nearest wall, his fist connecting with the ancient oak with a crack that sounded like a bone snapping.
His knuckles split instantly, crimson spattering the wallpaper.
"How could you?" he screamed, his voice cracking, raw from the battle and the betrayal. "How could you possibly look me in the eye today knowing what you did with that thing?"
Aurelia stood frozen in the center of the drawing room. She looked fragile, her skin pale beneath the grime, but there was a terrifying stillness in her posture.
"Theo, please. Sit down."
"You’re bleeding. You’re not thinking—"
"Don’t you dare tell me what I’m thinking!" Theo spun on her, his one good eye blazing with a psychotic intensity.
His pupils were blown wide, darting erratically as his mind fractured under the weight of the image he couldn’t erase: Rex’s cold, calculating hands on his mother.
"I saw him, Mother! I saw the way he looked at us!"
"He didn’t just take you; he owned you!"
"He used you like some fucking object, some disposable toy, and you let him!"
"It wasn’t like that," she whispered, though the tremor in her hands betrayed her.
"Then what was it like?" Theo’s laughter was jagged, hysterical. He began to pace the room like a caged predator, his movements twitchy and violent. "Was it love? Was it ’sacrifice’?!"
"Because it looked like surrender to me! You didn’t fight him!"
"You lay there while he dismantled everything we were... And now..." His voice dropped to a horrified whisper, his face contorting in disgust. "And now there’s his blood in you!
"His seed! You’re carrying a monster!"
"I did it to save us, Theo!" Aurelia finally snapped, her voice rising to match his desperation.
Tears streaked through the bloodstains on her cheeks. "The family was drowning!"
"The debts, the enemies, and the magical corruption where Rex offered a solution!"
"He offered stability, power, and protection. The price was... it was me."
"The price was your soul!" Theo shrieked, kicking a mahogany side table.
The wood splintered under his enhanced strength, sending shards flying across the room. "You traded yourself to a demon to buy us a few more years of breathing?!"
"Do you know what that makes us? We’re not a family anymore!"
"We’re his property! We’re his livestock!"
His breathing became shallow, rapid hyperventilation bordering on a full psychotic break. His inner monologue was a screaming cacophony.
’He’s watching. He’s listening through the walls.’
’He’s laughing because she gave up. He won. He fucked our lives apart, and she thanked him for it.

"You think you’re so righteous, standing there bleeding for a world that’s already dead," Aurelia said, stepping toward him, reaching out with unsteady hands. "You don’t understand the choices I had to make!"
"I chose survival over pride."
Theo recoiled from her touch as if her skin were molten lava. "Don’t touch me!"

"Don’t you fucking touch me with hands that he touched!" He grabbed a crystal vase from the mantel and hurled it at the fireplace. It shattered into a thousand glittering teeth. "Every time I look at you now, I won’t see my mother!"
"I’ll see his puppet. I’ll see the woman who knelt before a monster and asked for more."
"Theo, stop this madness--"

"Madness? This isn’t madness, this is clarity!" Theo’s face was a mask of pure, unadulterated rage, his veins standing out like cords on his neck. "The world is burning, Rex is standing in the ashes holding the match, and you’re inside here, carrying his fucking legacy!"
He grabbed his own hair, claws digging into his scalp. "I want to kill him. I want to rip his throat out and watch him choke on the blood of the family he corrupted."
He turned to her, his expression suddenly going eerily blank, the kind of calm that precedes a massacre. "But I can’t, can I?!"
"Because every time I try to strike him, I remember that I’d be striking the father of the thing growing inside you!"
"He’s rigged the game, Mother!"
"He didn’t just defeat us! He made us complicit!"
He collapsed to his knees, not in surrender, but as if the sheer gravity of his hatred had become too heavy to bear. He began to sob, not tears of sadness, but wet, choking sounds of rage.
"I hate you. God help me, I hate you more than I hate him."

chapters.title: Chapter 1054. Magnificent, the Variable Has Exceeded Expectations
paragraphs: The air in the drawing room became a pressurized chamber of violence. Theo wasn’t just angry anymore; he was unraveling.

The psychological wound inflicted by Rex’s cold pragmatism had torn a hole in his psyche that no amount of grief could patch. His mind was no longer his own; it was a battlefield where reality and hallucination fought for dominance.
’Kill her,’ a voice hissed in the back of his skull.
It wasn’t his own. It was ancient, oily, and hungry.
’She is the vessel of his corruption.’
’End the lineage.’
’End the taint.’
"Theo, please, you’re scaring me." Aurelia’s plea was the wrong thing to say.
To Theo’s fractured mind, her fear sounded like condescension. It sounded like she was patronizing him from her position of sinful surrender.
"Scaring you?" Theo’s laughter was a wet, broken sound. "You should be terrified!"
"You should be screaming until your lungs burst!"

Suddenly, his movements became a blur of unnatural speed. The temporal energy bleeding from his pores distorted the space around him, making him appear to stutter through reality like a broken film reel.
Before Aurelia could even gasp, his hands were around her throat.
"You gave him everything!" he screamed directly into her face, his grip tightening with bone-crushing force. "You gave him our dignity, our blood, our future!"
"If you want to be his toy, then die like one!"
Aurelia’s hands clawed uselessly at his wrists. Her face began to flush a deep, bruised purple, her eyes bulging as she fought for oxygen.
"Th-Theo," she managed to wheeze, the sound barely audible over the roaring of the temporal distortions.
’More power,’ Kaeleth whispered, the voice now a deafening crescendo in Theo’s mind. ’Feed the distortion.’
’Let time fracture.’
’Break the vessel, and you break the curse.’

Theo’s vision began to bleed crimson. The room started to warp; the walls seemed to stretch into infinite corridors of shadow, and the clock on the mantel began to tick backward with the sound of grinding teeth.
He could feel the power raw, chaotic, and terrifying surging through his veins. He felt like he could reach out and tear the seconds from the air.
He wanted to tear the very concept of ’now’ apart.
"I’ll end it!" Theo howled, his fingers sinking deeper into Aurelia’s flesh. "I’ll end the bloodline before his bastard can breathe!"
"THEO! STOP!
The door burst open with enough force to crack the frame. Morwenna charged into the room, her face a mask of desperate horror.
She didn’t hesitate; she threw herself forward, her hands grasping Theo’s wrists.
The contact was like touching live electricity. The temporal energy lashed out at her, stinging her skin, threatening to age her bones decades in a single second.
With a strength born of pure terror, Morwenna wrenched his hands away from Aurelia’s throat. Aurelia collapsed to the floor, gasping and retching as she fought to reclaim her breath.
"Theo, look at me!" Morwenna commanded, grabbing his shoulders, trying to anchor him to the present. "This isn’t you!"
"This is what he wanted! He wanted you to break!"
But Theo didn’t look at her. His eyes were rolled back, showing only bloodshot whites.
His body was vibrating with such intensity that the floorboards beneath him began to splinter and splinter further.
"It’s too late, Morwenna," a voice whispered, but it wasn’t Kaeleth.
It was the realization dawning in Morwenna’s own heart.
She looked at her grandson. She saw the way his shadow moved independently of his body, twisting like something alive.
She saw the way the air around him cracked like broken glass. She saw the hollowed-out shell of the boy she loved, replaced by a weapon designed by Rex Rexilion.

Rex hadn’t just manipulated events; he had orchestrated a symphony of destruction where every note was a tragedy. He had provoked the trauma, fed the resentment, and now he sat back while the pieces tore each other apart.
"Theo..." Morwenna’s voice broke. "Please, my great-grandson..."

"Great-grandson?" Theo’s head snapped toward her. When he spoke, his voice sounded layered, as if three people were speaking at once his own, Kaeleth’s, and something ancient and dead. "There is no grandson here, Grandmother."
"Only survivors. And only victims."

The temporal field expanded. A shockwave of distorted time rippled outward from Theo, shattering the windows and sending furniture flying. Morwenna fell back, shielding her face as the room began to dissolve into a kaleidoscope of fractured moments.

As she watched Theo’s face contort into something inhuman, something utterly lost to the darkness, Morwenna realized the terrible truth. Rex hadn’t just won the battle; he had won the war for their souls.
Hope wasn’t just dying; it had been systematically dismantled, leaving nothing behind but the cold, inevitable victory of the monster.
"I’LL END IT ALL!!!" Theo let out a massive rage that caused an explosion.
The explosion did not come from fire or gunpowder; it came from the fundamental unraveling of causality itself.
Inside the drawing room, Theo’s scream transcended the audible spectrum. It became a physical force, a psychic shriek that tore through the fabric of the moment.

His rage was no longer a human emotion; it had become a gravitational event. The temporal energy hemorrhaging from his body reached critical mass, feeding off the hatred that burned in his marrow, the disgust he felt for his mother’s complicity, and the murderous fury directed at the man who had orchestrated their ruin.
"I WILL TEAR THE SECONDS FROM YOUR BONES!" Theo roared, but the words didn’t travel through the air; they vibrated through time itself.
The world convulsed. A sphere of distorted reality erupted from Theo’s center, expanding outward with the inevitability of a supernova.
In an instant, the screaming stopped. The shattering glass froze midair, each shard suspended like a diamond in amber.
Morwenna’s outstretched hand remained locked in space; Aurelia’s gasping mouth was stilled in a silent plea for mercy. The very dust motes in the air became motionless stars.
Time did not simply slow down; it died. The universe within the radius of Theo’s wrath became a tomb of frozen moments.
Miles away, or perhaps mere seconds away, for time had lost all meaning, Rex Rexilion stopped mid-stride in the academy corridors. He did not flinch, and he did not panic.
Instead, he tilted his head slightly, a faint, almost imperceptible smile touching his lips. He could feel it.
The sudden, violent stagnation in the temporal flow. It felt like a pulse of pure, concentrated venom cutting through the ether.
’Magnificent,’ Rex thought. ’The variable has exceeded expectations.’
’The rage has achieved transcendence. ’
Back in the courtyard, the frozen world was a grotesque gallery of suffering. But at the epicenter, Theo was not frozen.
He was moving through the stillness like a god of calamity. His eyes were twin vortexes of chronological decay, swirling with gold and black energy.
Every step he took left cracks in the air itself, visible fissures where reality had been torn apart by his sheer presence.
He was a creature of pure, unadulterated hatred. His mind was a storm of images: Rex’s face, the pregnant belly of his mother, the broken walls, the blood on the cobblestones.
Every memory was fuel. Every tear he had shed was now a weapon. He wasn’t just angry at Rex; he was angry at the very concept of a world where Rex Rexilion was allowed to exist.
He wanted to reach into the clockwork of the universe and grind the gears to dust.

The temporal freeze was not a shield; it was his domain. In this silent, motionless wasteland, Theo was the only thing that was truly alive, and his life was defined entirely by the desire to destroy.
Eventually, the pressure began to subside, not because the rage had faded, but because it had exhausted the immediate capacity of the local reality to bend further.
The distortion began to contract, pulling back toward the source like a dying star.
Theo emerged from the household’s interior approximately ninety minutes after Aurelia had steered him inside.

The emergence was the specific emergence of someone who had spent ninety minutes in a space with people who cared about them and had received what the caring people had to give and had found that what they had to give was real and insufficient simultaneously.

He had been met with tears, with desperate embraces, with hollow apologies that could not undo the violation of their bloodline. He had processed the grief; he had processed the betrayal, and he had found that the residue, the raw, jagged hatred, was still there, stronger than before.

He stepped out into the courtyard, his boots crunching on the frozen debris. He stood in the specific state of someone who had processed what was processable and had found that the residue was still there.
His face was no longer contorted in rage; it was something far more terrifying: it was cold. It was the stillness of a blade before the strike.
He stared toward the Academy, his gaze piercing through the walls, seeking the one man whose existence was an insult to every heartbeat Theo possessed.

The shattering glass froze midair, each shard suspended like a diamond in amber.
Morwenna’s outstretched hand remained locked in space; Aurelia’s gasping mouth was stilled in a silent plea for mercy.
The very dust motes in the air became motionless stars.
Time did not simply slow down; it died.
The universe within the radius of Theo’s wrath became a tomb of frozen moments.
Miles away, or perhaps mere seconds away, for time had lost all meaning, Rex Rexilion stopped mid-stride in the academy corridors.
He did not flinch, and he did not panic.
Instead, he tilted his head slightly, a faint, almost imperceptible smile touching his lips.
He could feel it.
The sudden, violent stagnation in the temporal flow.
It felt like a pulse of pure, concentrated venom cutting through the ether.
’Magnificent,’ Rex thought. ’The variable has exceeded expectations.’
’The rage has achieved transcendence. ’
Back in the courtyard, the frozen world was a grotesque gallery of suffering.
But at the epicenter, Theo was not frozen.
He was moving through the stillness like a god of calamity.
His eyes were twin vortexes of chronological decay, swirling with gold and black energy.
Every step he took left cracks in the air itself, visible fissures where reality had been torn apart by his sheer presence.
He was a creature of pure, unadulterated hatred.
His mind was a storm of images: Rex’s face, the pregnant belly of his mother, the broken walls, the blood on the cobblestones.
Every memory was fuel.
Every tear he had shed was now a weapon.
He wasn’t just angry at Rex; he was angry at the very concept of a world where Rex Rexilion was allowed to exist.
He wanted to reach into the clockwork of the universe and grind the gears to dust.
The temporal freeze was not a shield; it was his domain.
In this silent, motionless wasteland, Theo was the only thing that was truly alive, and his life was defined entirely by the desire to destroy.
Eventually, the pressure began to subside, not because the rage had faded, but because it had exhausted the immediate capacity of the local reality to bend further.
The distortion began to contract, pulling back toward the source like a dying star.
Theo emerged from the household’s interior approximately ninety minutes after Aurelia had steered him inside.

The emergence was the specific emergence of someone who had spent ninety minutes in a space with people who cared about them and had received what the caring people had to give and had found that what they had to give was real and insufficient simultaneously.
He had been met with tears, with desperate embraces, with hollow apologies that could not undo the violation of their bloodline.
He had processed the grief; he had processed the betrayal, and he had found that the residue, the raw, jagged hatred, was still there, stronger than before.
He stepped out into the courtyard, his boots crunching on the frozen debris.
He stood in the specific state of someone who had processed what was processable and had found that the residue was still there.
His face was no longer contorted in rage; it was something far more terrifying: it was cold.
It was the stillness of a blade before the strike.
He stared toward the Academy, his gaze piercing through the walls, seeking the one man whose existence was an insult to every heartbeat Theo possessed.

chapters.title: Chapter 1055. Take It Over My Dead Body
paragraphs: The courtyard of the Nightwing estate was no longer a place of training; it was a consecrated ground for a massacre. The air itself felt brittle, as if the atmosphere had been crystallized by the sheer force of Theo’s lingering temporal distortion.

Rex Rexilion stood in the center of the training circle, his movements precise, almost hypnotic. He moved through the mastery’s martial forms, a flowing sequence of deadly transitions designed to maintain the body’s combat memory.
Each strike was silent, each shift of weight absolute. He looked less like a man practicing and more like a predator maintaining its edge.
Theo watched from the shadows of the colonnade. His breathing was ragged, each inhale feeling like he was swallowing broken glass.
His knuckles were still split and weeping blood, but he didn’t feel the pain. All he felt was the white-hot, pulsing hatred that had become his new heartbeat.
His mind was a fractured mirror, reflecting only one image: Rex’s face.
"I know what you are," Theo spat.
His voice didn’t carry across the courtyard; it seemed to tear through the silence like a blade.

Rex completed a devastating circular transition, his palm stopping millimeters from an imaginary throat, before he settled into a perfect stance. He didn’t turn immediately. He allowed the silence to stretch, a deliberate provocation.
"You said that earlier, Theo."
"I mean it differently now," Theo said, stepping into the light. His eyes were bloodshot, pupils dilated into pinpricks of murderous intent. "Before, I was an accusation."
"A child crying out against an injustice."
"Now?" He let out a laugh that sounded like bones grinding together. "Now, I am a statement of fact."
"I am the consequence you created."
Rex finally turned. His expression was unnervingly placid, the flat, patient attention of a god observing an insect.
"And what is this statement?"
"That I am a vector," Theo snarled, stalking forward. "As long as I carry this designation, as long as Kaeleth’s voice screams in my skull, I am the weapon you forged to destroy yourself."
"I am the plague you invited into your house."
"Yes," Rex said simply.
The casual acceptance was like salt in a wound.
"And you are going to address that." Theo’s voice rose, cracking with restrained insanity. "You’re going to take it."
Rex’s eyes narrowed almost imperceptibly. "Take what?"
"The designation!" Theo screamed, the temporal energy around him flaring, causing the pebbles at his feet to levitate and shatter. "You think I don’t see it?!"
"You think I’m too broken to understand your fucking calculus?!"
"You’ve been hunting Kaeleth since before this month began!"
"You’ve been playing this long game, sacrificing families, sacrificing souls, sacrificing my mother!"

Theo’s fist slammed into a stone pillar beside him, the impact sending a shockwave through the courtyard. "The designation I was given was temporal mechanics, the navigational component—it was the last piece of your puzzle!"
"You didn’t want to kill me; you wanted to study me!"
"You wanted to adapt to the designation’s mechanics so you could navigate to Kaeleth’s domain!"
"You needed the key, and you used my trauma to forge it!
Rex said nothing. His silence was a vacuum, sucking the air out of Theo’s lungs.

"You want to use dimensional manipulation and presence manipulation to breach his realm," Theo continued, his words coming faster now, fueled by a psychotic frenzy. "And you need the temporal designation’s navigational data to find the coordinates."
"You need to bridge the gap between our reality and his."
"Hohhh...?" Rex smirked. "Busted, huh?"
"But I don’t care as long as he’s aware of me trying to get to his ass," Rex laughed. "Then this is indeed going to make everything interesting."
Theo stopped inches from Rex’s face. The hatred between them was so potent it felt like a physical barrier.
Theo’s breath smelled of copper and rage. "You want the power of a god to go to war with a demon. So take it. Take it from me."
Rex’s hand moved in a blur of motion that Theo barely registered and gripped Theo’s throat. It wasn’t a killing blow but a test of will.
"You think you can simply hand over something that has rewritten your very existence?"
Theo didn’t flinch. He leaned into the grip, his eyes burning with a terrifying smile. "I’m not handing it to you, you bastard."
"I’m forcing it on you. I am giving you the very thing that will consume you."
Rex’s grip tightened, his fingers digging into the muscle of Theo’s neck. "You want to die for this? To be a hollow shell so I can have my war?"
"I want you to feel it," Theo whispered, his voice dripping with venom. "I want you to feel the weight of every soul you’ve crushed."
"I want you to take this designation and feel Kaeleth’s fingers tightening around your throat!"
"I want you to take it over my dead body."
The tension in the courtyard reached a breaking point. The air screamed as the two forces, Rex’s cold, calculated ambition and Theo’s raw, chaotic hatred, collided.
"Then come and claim it," Rex said, his voice dropping to a lethal register. "Try to take it from me."
Theo’s response was not words. It was a roar of pure, unbridled violence as he swung a fist imbued with the power to shatter time itself.

The collision was not merely physical; it was a cataclysmic rupture in the fabric of the present. When Theo’s fist connected with Rex’s forearm, the sound wasn’t a wet thud; it was a CRACK BOOM, like a lightning strike trapped inside a bell.
The temporal shockwave rippled outward, pulverizing the stone tiles beneath them into fine white powder.
Theo didn’t stop. He couldn’t stop.
He was a hurricane of grief and chronological fury.
’FUCK YOU!’ Theo’s mind screamed, drowning out the divine whispers of Kaeleth. ’FUCK EVERYTHING YOU’VE BUILT!’

He unleashed a torrent of temporal energy, his movements becoming a series of staccato blurs. To any observer, Theo would seem to be teleporting, but in reality, he was simply accelerating his own personal timeline to impossible speeds.
He struck Rex with three consecutive blows: a left hook, an uppercut, and a spinning backfist, each hit landing with the force of a freight train.
THWACK CRUNCH!
Rex’s head snapped back from the first blow, blood spraying from his split lip in a crimson arc. But as Theo pivoted for the second strike, Rex moved.
He didn’t dodge; he simply shifted his presence, his body flickering like a flame in a draft. Theo’s fist passed through the space Rex had occupied, finding only empty air.
"Is that all your hatred provides, Theo?" Rex’s voice came from behind him, cold and mocking. "Raw, directionless momentum?"
"SHUT UP!" Theo roared.
He spun, his hand glowing with a sickly gold light. He grabbed the air itself and pulled.
VROOOOM SHATTER!
The space around Rex fractured. Time slowed to a crawl within a three-foot radius of Rex, forcing his movements to become sluggish as if he were moving through molten lead.
Seizing the opening, Theo drove his knee into Rex’s ribs.
CRACK.
The sound of Rex’s ribcage splintering was sickeningly clear. Blood coughed from Rex’s mouth, spattering Theo’s face. But Rex didn’t collapse.
He grabbed Theo’s throat with both hands, his fingers like iron bands.
"You think pain is a currency I respect?" Rex growled, his eyes burning with a cold, predatory light.
Rex unleashed his own power, a surge of dimensional manipulation that twisted the space between them. Suddenly, Theo felt as though he were being pulled in two directions at once.
His left arm felt like it was stretching toward next week, while his right arm felt anchored in yesterday. The vertigo was nauseating.
"AUGH GAAAAH!" Theo screamed as his tendons strained against the temporal shear.
But the pain only fed the furnace. Theo’s eyes turned entirely gold.
"YOU WANT THE DESIGNATION?" he shrieked, his voice echoing with the layered distortion of Kaeleth’s power. "THEN FEEL THE FULL WEIGHT OF IT!"
Theo detonated his power outward in a sphere of chronological decay.
KRA KOOOOM!
The explosion threw Rex backward twenty feet, sending him skidding across the courtyard, leaving deep furrows in the earth.
Theo didn’t give him a moment to breathe. He charged, his footsteps sounding like rapid-fire gunshots: tap, tap, tap, tap, tap!
Each step brought him closer to Rex in a series of microteleports.
Rex rose to one knee, wiping blood from his chin, his breathing heavy but controlled. As Theo closed the distance, Rex raised both hands.
"Presence Manipulation: Absolute Anchor."
The air around Rex became impossibly dense. When Theo swung a devastating overhead strike, it felt like he was trying to punch through solid diamond.
The impact sent a shockwave up Theo’s arm that threatened to shatter his own radius and ulna.
KRA THOOM!
"Too slow," Rex whispered. He drove a palm into Theo’s solar plexus.
The impact wasn’t just physical; it was a dimensional displacement that momentarily displaced Theo’s internal organs, sending him spiraling backward in agony.
Theo hit the ground hard, gasping for air that felt too thin to breathe. His vision swam.
His ribs felt like broken shards of glass grinding against each other. But through the haze of pain, he saw Rex walking toward him, methodical and inexorable.
’Don’t stop,’ Kaeleth whispered, the voice now a seductive purr. ’Break him.’
’Break the world.’
’Let time bleed until there is nothing left but the void.’
"I’m not... done..." Theo wheezed.

chapters.title: Chapter 1056. Screaming at the Universe for Not Obeying
paragraphs: He forced himself up, blood streaming from his nose and ears. His skin was beginning to crack as the temporal energy leaked from his pores like steam from a pressure cooker.
"You’re just... the beginning, Rex."

Theo clenched his fists, and the ground beneath him began to age and decay in real time, turning from solid stone to crumbling sand in seconds. The air began to hum with a high-pitched, lethal frequency.
"Come on then," Theo challenged, his voice a guttural snarl. "Come and take it from my corpse!"
The courtyard had ceased to exist as a physical location; it was now a kaleidoscopic nightmare of fractured causality. Theo was no longer fighting like a man; he was fighting like a catastrophe.
"CHRONOS EROSION!" Theo screamed, thrusting both palms forward.
A wave of accelerated time erupted from his hands. Anything the energy touched—the stone pillars, the fallen debris, even the air itself—aged centuries in a heartbeat.
The stone crumbled into fine dust instantly. Rex, caught in the direct path, felt his skin blister and crack as his cellular age was forcibly accelerated.
Sssssss CRACK!
But before the dust could even settle, Rex’s body reacted. A pale, ethereal glow erupted from his wounds.

The cracked skin fused shut; the cellular damage reversed as his Supreme Healing worked in perfect synchronization with his Infinite Regeneration. The wounds didn’t just heal; they rewrote themselves, stronger and more resilient to the specific frequency of the temporal decay.
Rex stepped through the cloud of dust, his eyes glowing with an adaptive intensity.
"Interesting," Rex muttered, his voice unnervingly calm despite the blood still trickling from his ears. "My biology is already recalibrating to the temporal decay constant."
"I can feel the clockwork trying to unravel me, and I am simply... refusing."
"REFUSE THIS THEN!" Theo roared, his rage reaching a fever pitch.
He vanished.
SHING SHING SHING!
Theo reappeared in three places at once, temporal afterimages so solid they possessed mass. He struck Rex from three directions simultaneously.
A kick to the temple, a palm strike to the sternum, and a bladed hand aimed at the throat.
THUD, CRUNCH, SLASH!
Rex took the hits. His jaw twisted sideways from the kick, his ribs shattered under the palm strike, and a thin line of blood appeared across his throat.
But as he stumbled, his body flickered. The damage was already knitting together behind the strike.
He was adapting in real time, his nervous system learning the timing of Theo’s afterimages.
Rex caught Theo’s wrist mid-swing. "Got you."
The counterattack was brutal. Rex drove an elbow into Theo’s face, then spun, using Theo’s own momentum to hurl him against the crumbling wall.
BOOM!
Theo coughed up a glob of blood, but as he hit the wall, he triggered the Temporal Stasis Field. The space between him and Rex became viscous, like invisible molasses.
Rex’s advance slowed to a crawl, his movements becoming agonizingly labored.
"You think you’re invincible?" Theo hissed, rising like a demon from the rubble. "I’ll peel back your layers until there’s nothing left to regenerate!
Theo unleashed a barrage of techniques that defied physics:
"DECOHERENCE STRIKE! "A punch that hit Rex three seconds before Theo’s fist actually connected.
"PARADOX SHIELD!" A barrier that redirected Rex’s own kinetic energy back at him.
"EVENT HORIZON BURST!" A localized implosion of time that tried to crush Rex into a single point of infinite density.
VROOOOM KRA KOOM!

The courtyard sounded like a war zone of collapsing dimensions. Each time Rex was beaten to the brink of death, his bones splintered into powder, and his organs liquefied by temporal pressure; the Supreme Healing would kick in with terrifying efficiency.
Rex would stand up, his muscles denser, his reflexes sharper, his very essence adapting to the specific magical signature of every move Theo threw at him.
Inside the shared consciousness of the designation, Kaeleth’s presence stirred. The ancient entity wasn’t just observing; it was calculating.
’This is... problematic,’ Kaeleth’s voice echoed in the back of Theo’s mind, cold and calculating. ’The vessel is not merely surviving; he is evolving.’
’Every wound is a lesson he is learning from your rage.’
’He is becoming a perfect counter to your existence, Theo.’
’If you continue this direct assault, you will only feed his ascension.’
"I DON’T CARE ABOUT EVOLUTION!" Theo screamed aloud, his eyes leaking golden temporal fluid. "I WANT HIM DEAD!"
Theo gathered every ounce of his remaining power. The air around him began to scream as he prepared his most desperate gambit:
"THE END OF ALL SECONDS." He attempted to freeze Rex in a permanent moment of nonexistence, a temporal prison from which no regeneration could escape.
Rex stood in the center of the swirling chaos, his breathing steadying even as his body underwent constant, violent reconstruction. His mind was working faster than his body.
He saw the pattern. He saw the way Theo’s power ebbed and flowed with his emotional state.
’He’s running out of fuel,’ Rex realized, watching the golden glow of Theo’s aura flicker. ’His rage is infinite, but his body’s ability to channel it is finite.’
’I don’t need to kill him yet... I need to exhaust the source.’

Rex lowered his stance, not to attack, but to endure. He prepared to absorb the next impossible blow, his regeneration primed to handle the next level of devastation, waiting for the exact microsecond when Theo’s hatred would finally meet its limit.
"Come, Theo," Rex said, blood dripping from his chin as he smiled a predator’s smile. "Show me how much more of yourself you’re willing to burn to kill me."

The courtyard had become a graveyard of causality. The ground was no longer stone or dirt; it was a shifting slurry of ancient dust and futuristic metal fragments, caught in a perpetual loop of decay and reconstruction.
Theo was beyond rage now. He had passed through anger, through grief, and landed somewhere far more dangerous: pure, unadulterated frustration.
His movements were no longer graceful; they were frantic, desperate bursts of violence. He was a man trying to strangle time itself, and time was slipping through his fingers.
"WHY WON’T YOU JUST DIE?!" Theo screamed, the sound tearing from his throat like raw meat being ripped apart. "DIE! DIE! DIE!"
He unleashed a cascade of temporal torment. "CHRONO SHREDDER SPEAR!"

He thrust his fingers forward, sending invisible lances of accelerated aging toward Rex’s vital organs. Each spear struck with the sound of tearing fabric, SHRIIIIIP, SHRIIIIIP piercing through flesh, liquefying muscle, and shattering bone.
Rex’s body was being torn apart in real time. A spear pierced his lung; another shattered his femur; a third liquefied his spleen.
Blood sprayed across the wasteland of the courtyard in grotesque, arterial fountains.
SPLUTCH CRUNCH.
But then, the laughter started.
It wasn’t a happy laugh. It was a low, guttural chuckle that vibrated through the very air, emerging from Rex’s blood-soaked throat.
As the spears struck him, Rex’s Full Potential Adaptation surged to its absolute zenith. His cells weren’t just healing; they were learning the exact atomic frequency of the temporal energy.
The wounds didn’t just close; they sealed with a reinforced, temporal-resistant barrier.
"Is that it?" Rex asked, his voice dripping with a terrifying, almost ecstatic amusement.
He stepped forward, walking through a stream of temporal energy that should have reduced him to ash. "You’re throwing tantrums, Theo!"
"You’re screaming at the universe because it won’t obey your tantrum."
Theo’s face contorted. His eyes burned with a gold so bright it was painful to look at.
"I’LL TEAR THE TIME FROM YOUR VERY BONES!"
Theo launched into a suicidal assault. He moved so fast he became a continuous line of golden light, a blur of endless strikes.
"TEMPORAL OVERLOAD: ZERO SECOND STRIKE!" Each punch landed with the force of a collapsing star.
BOOM CRACK BOOM CRACK BOOM!
Rex was being pummeled into the earth. His jaw was dislocated, his nose was crushed flat, and his ribs were reduced to splinters that pierced his own heart.
But with every devastating blow, Rex’s laughter grew louder. The pain was no longer an obstacle; it was data.
Each broken bone taught his body how to brace against the shockwave; each ruptured organ taught his regeneration how to preempt the next rupture.
HA HA HA HA HA!
Rex’s laughter echoed off the crumbling walls of the estate. "Yes! More! Give me more of this delicious agony!"
"Every time you break me, you make me more perfect!"
"You’re not fighting me, Theo; you’re building me!"
The psychological torment was worse than the physical. Theo felt his grip on reality slipping.
He was pouring everything, his hatred, his trauma, his very soul, into these attacks, and Rex was simply... consuming it.
Rex was a black hole of adaptation, turning Theo’s genocide-level power into his own evolutionary fuel.
Theo’s breathing became a series of wet, panicked gasps. His golden aura began to flicker violently, revealing the exhaustion beneath the rage.
His muscles screamed, his nervous system was fried from channeling so much raw temporal energy, and his mind was fracturing under the weight of Rex’s mocking mirth.
"ONE LAST TIME!" Theo shrieked, his voice cracking into a high-pitched wail. "THIS IS THE END OF YOUR STORY! "
Theo gathered every remaining drop of Kaeleth’s power. The air around him began to warp and bend, creating a vacuum that pulled debris toward him.

His fists glowed with an unstable, blinding white-gold light, a concentrated singularity of temporal force. He threw himself forward in one final, desperate gambit, a punch designed to erase Rex from every timeline simultaneously.
"FINAL PARADOX: OBLIVION STRIKE!"

"You’re just... the beginning, Rex."
Theo clenched his fists, and the ground beneath him began to age and decay in real time, turning from solid stone to crumbling sand in seconds.
The air began to hum with a high-pitched, lethal frequency.
"Come on then," Theo challenged, his voice a guttural snarl.
"Come and take it from my corpse!"
The courtyard had ceased to exist as a physical location; it was now a kaleidoscopic nightmare of fractured causality.
Theo was no longer fighting like a man; he was fighting like a catastrophe.
"CHRONOS EROSION!" Theo screamed, thrusting both palms forward.
A wave of accelerated time erupted from his hands.
Anything the energy touched—the stone pillars, the fallen debris, even the air itself—aged centuries in a heartbeat.
The stone crumbled into fine dust instantly.
Rex, caught in the direct path, felt his skin blister and crack as his cellular age was forcibly accelerated.
Sssssss CRACK!
But before the dust could even settle, Rex’s body reacted.
A pale, ethereal glow erupted from his wounds.
The cracked skin fused shut; the cellular damage reversed as his Supreme Healing worked in perfect synchronization with his Infinite Regeneration.
The wounds didn’t just heal; they rewrote themselves, stronger and more resilient to the specific frequency of the temporal decay.
Rex stepped through the cloud of dust, his eyes glowing with an adaptive intensity.
"Interesting," Rex muttered, his voice unnervingly calm despite the blood still trickling from his ears.
"My biology is already recalibrating to the temporal decay constant."
"I can feel the clockwork trying to unravel me, and I am simply... refusing."
"REFUSE THIS THEN!" Theo roared, his rage reaching a fever pitch.
He vanished.
SHING SHING SHING!
Theo reappeared in three places at once, temporal afterimages so solid they possessed mass.
He struck Rex from three directions simultaneously.
A kick to the temple, a palm strike to the sternum, and a bladed hand aimed at the throat.
THUD, CRUNCH, SLASH!
Rex took the hits.
His jaw twisted sideways from the kick, his ribs shattered under the palm strike, and a thin line of blood appeared across his throat.
But as he stumbled, his body flickered.
The damage was already knitting together behind the strike.
He was adapting in real time, his nervous system learning the timing of Theo’s afterimages.
Rex caught Theo’s wrist mid-swing.
"Got you."
The counterattack was brutal.
Rex drove an elbow into Theo’s face, then spun, using Theo’s own momentum to hurl him against the crumbling wall.
BOOM!

The space between him and Rex became viscous, like invisible molasses.
Rex’s advance slowed to a crawl, his movements becoming agonizingly labored.
"You think you’re invincible?" Theo hissed, rising like a demon from the rubble.
"I’ll peel back your layers until there’s nothing left to regenerate!
Theo unleashed a barrage of techniques that defied physics:
"DECOHERENCE STRIKE!

"PARADOX SHIELD!" A barrier that redirected Rex’s own kinetic energy back at him.
"EVENT HORIZON BURST!" A localized implosion of time that tried to crush Rex into a single point of infinite density.
VROOOOM KRA KOOM!
The courtyard sounded like a war zone of collapsing dimensions.
Each time Rex was beaten to the brink of death, his bones splintered into powder, and his organs liquefied by temporal pressure; the Supreme Healing would kick in with terrifying efficiency.
Rex would stand up, his muscles denser, his reflexes sharper, his very essence adapting to the specific magical signature of every move Theo threw at him.
Inside the shared consciousness of the designation, Kaeleth’s presence stirred.
The ancient entity wasn’t just observing; it was calculating.
’This is... problematic,’ Kaeleth’s voice echoed in the back of Theo’s mind, cold and calculating. ’The vessel is not merely surviving; he is evolving.’
’Every wound is a lesson he is learning from your rage.’
’He is becoming a perfect counter to your existence, Theo.’
’If you continue this direct assault, you will only feed his ascension.’
"I DON’T CARE ABOUT EVOLUTION!" Theo screamed aloud, his eyes leaking golden temporal fluid.
"I WANT HIM DEAD!"
Theo gathered every ounce of his remaining power.
The air around him began to scream as he prepared his most desperate gambit:
"THE END OF ALL SECONDS." He attempted to freeze Rex in a permanent moment of nonexistence, a temporal prison from which no regeneration could escape.
Rex stood in the center of the swirling chaos, his breathing steadying even as his body underwent constant, violent reconstruction.
His mind was working faster than his body.
He saw the pattern.
He saw the way Theo’s power ebbed and flowed with his emotional state.
’He’s running out of fuel,’ Rex realized, watching the golden glow of Theo’s aura flicker. ’His rage is infinite, but his body’s ability to channel it is finite.’
’I don’t need to kill him yet...
I need to exhaust the source.’
Rex lowered his stance, not to attack, but to endure.
He prepared to absorb the next impossible blow, his regeneration primed to handle the next level of devastation, waiting for the exact microsecond when Theo’s hatred would finally meet its limit.

Blood sprayed across the wasteland of the courtyard in grotesque, arterial fountains.

It wasn’t a happy laugh.
It was a low, guttural chuckle that vibrated through the very air, emerging from Rex’s blood-soaked throat.
As the spears struck him, Rex’s Full Potential Adaptation surged to its absolute zenith.
His cells weren’t just healing; they were learning the exact atomic frequency of the temporal energy.
The wounds didn’t just close; they sealed with a reinforced, temporal-resistant barrier.

More!

chapters.title: Chapter 1057. Let’s Give Them a Show They’ll Never Forget
paragraphs: The world went silent. For a heartbeat, even the wind stopped.
The attack moved faster than light, a streak of absolute annihilation aimed directly at Rex’s sternum.
But Rex didn’t flinch. He didn’t dodge.
He didn’t even raise his hands to guard. He simply stood his ground, his eyes locked onto Theo’s with a cold, terrifying clarity.
His adaptation had reached its limit. He knew exactly what this move was.
He knew its speed, its mass, and its temporal signature.
As the fist of annihilation drew within an inch of his chest, Rex moved.
It wasn’t a blur; it was a statement of absolute dominance. With precise, economical motion, Rex raised his left hand.
CLANG.

The sound wasn’t a crash or an explosion; it was the sound of two immovable objects meeting. Rex’s palm met Theo’s glowing fist mid-strike, catching the full force of the oblivion strike with impossible ease.
The shockwave rippled outward through the ground, cracking the earth in a perfect circle around them, but Rex’s arm didn’t even tremble.
The golden light of the attack died against Rex’s skin. The silence that followed was deafening.

Rex’s palm held Theo’s fist fast, the two men frozen in a tableau of absolute power and absolute desperation. Rex leaned forward slightly, his face splattered with blood but his expression utterly serene.
"My turn," Rex whispered.
The silence that followed the impact was more terrifying than the explosions that preceded it. Theo’s eyes, wide and bloodshot, stared into Rex’s pupils.
He could feel the power of the Oblivion Strike, the attack meant to erase existence, simply bleeding away into Rex’s palm like water into sand.
Rex’s grip tightened slightly, not enough to break bones, but enough to remind Theo who owned the space they stood in.
"You’re exhausted, Theo," Rex said softly, his voice carrying an almost patronizing tenderness. "Your timeline is fraying at the edges."
"You’ve spent everything on a lie."
Theo tried to pull away, to trigger another burst of temporal energy, but nothing happened. When he tried to accelerate his own time to escape the grip, he felt nothing but a dull ache.
His magic wasn’t just failing; it was being actively rejected by the space around Rex. His Full Potential Adaptation had reached its final stage: temporal immunity.
"Impossible..." Theo wheezed, blood bubbling between his lips. "I am the end of all things... I am the clock that stops..."
"No," Rex interrupted, releasing Theo’s fist with a dismissive flick. "You’re just a boy playing with a broken watch."
Rex moved.
It wasn’t a fight anymore; it was a demonstration. Theo swung a desperate, wild haymaker.
Rex didn’t even seem to move; he simply leaned an inch to the left, letting the fist whistle past his ear.
WHOOSH.
Before Theo could recover, Rex delivered a lightning-fast flick to Theo’s forehead.
TOCK.
It sounded like a clock ticking. The force sent Theo spinning backward, his head snapping back.
Before he could hit the ground, Rex appeared beside him, grabbing him by the collar.
"Let’s try something different," Rex mused. "Since you love time so much, let’s see how you handle its absence."
Rex unleashed a controlled burst of dimensional compression. He didn’t hit Theo; he hit the space around Theo.
The air suddenly became as solid as steel, boxing Theo in a transparent, crushing cage of distorted reality.
CRUNCH.
Theo screamed as the compressed space began to squeeze his ribs. He tried to use temporal stasis to freeze the pressure, but the magic fizzled out like a dying candle.
Rex’s adaptation had already mapped the frequency of Theo’s stasis; the universe now simply refused to let Theo slow down anything within Rex’s immediate influence.
Rex walked up to the invisible barrier, tapping on it with a finger.
Tink. Tink.
"Look at you," Rex mocked, watching Theo struggle against the invisible walls. "The great harbinger of decay, trapped in a moment of his own making."
"You’re not a god, Theo. You’re just a glitch in my system."
Desperate, Theo gathered every last spark of Kaeleth’s essence. "I’LL KILL YOU! I’LL ERASE THE VERY CONCEPT OF YOU!"
He punched at the barrier, unleashing a Chronos Singularity, a black hole of temporal force aimed directly at Rex’s face.
VROOOOOM WHUMP.
The singularity formed, a swirling vortex of darkness that promised to devour all light and sound. It expanded toward Rex, a maw of absolute nothingness.

Rex didn’t even blink. As the singularity touched him, his skin rippled with a silver sheen, his full potential adaptation recognizing the threat and instantly generating a dimensional anchor that rendered the singularity harmless.
The black hole simply washed over him like harmless water, dissipating harmlessly against his skin.
Rex reached through the collapsing singularity as if it were a curtain of silk. His hand emerged unscathed, grasping Theo’s throat through the barrier.
SHATTER.
Rex broke the dimensional cage with raw strength, dragging a gasping, terrified Theo out into the open air. Theo’s legs gave out, and he collapsed to his knees at Rex’s feet.
The golden glow that had once defined him was now a sickly, flickering amber.
"Please..." Theo whispered, the word tasting like ash. "Make it stop..."
Rex crouched down, bringing his face level with Theo’s. The predator was done playing with its prey, but he wasn’t finished humiliating it. "Make what stop? The pain?"
"Or the realization that you never stood a chance?"
Rex raised a fist, not for a killing blow, but for a precise strike aimed at Theo’s solar plexus, a strike designed to maximize pain without causing unconsciousness.
"This is the lesson, Theo," Rex said, his eyes glowing with cold satisfaction. "Adaptation isn’t about surviving the storm."
"It’s about becoming the storm."
WHAM.

The blow landed with the precision of a surgeon and the force of a sledgehammer, sending Theo’s consciousness spiraling into a dark, screaming void, while Rex stood over him, the undisputed master of the present, the past, and the future.

Rex stood over the broken form of Theo, but his eyes weren’t on the boy. They were fixed on something far more interesting: the raw, untamed temporal energy still hemorrhaging from Theo’s fractured soul.
Rex could feel it, the golden ichor of time itself, leaking into the atmosphere.
A cruel smile spread across Rex’s face. He wasn’t just going to defeat Theo; he was going to dismantle his entire legacy.
He was going to turn Theo’s own power into the weapon that would execute his reputation.
"You wanted to control time, Theo," Rex whispered, leaning close enough that his breath stirred Theo’s matted hair. "But you never understood its most cruel property: it remembers."
Rex reached out, but he didn’t strike. His fingers sank into Theo’s chest as if passing through water.
This was Soul Manipulation fused with Adaptive Mimicry. Rex wasn’t just touching Theo; he was threading his own consciousness into the boy’s magical core.
Sssssss VROOOOM.

A sound like tearing parchment echoed through the courtyard as Rex forcibly synchronized his heartbeat with Theo’s magical pulse. He began to siphon the temporal essence, not to use it for himself, but to redirect its flow.
While Apollo remained trapped in a trance of temporal feedback from the earlier clash, Rex began to weave a web of deception.
Using Theo’s own signature, Rex sent microscopic pulses of temporal energy throughout the city of Aethelgard. To anyone watching, it would appear as though Theo’s power was lashing out involuntarily.
SPLAT. CRUNCH.
In the residential districts, shadows moved with terrifying speed. A child playing in an alleyway suddenly froze as a temporal blade mimicking Theo’s exact magical frequency sliced through the air.
SHING!
The child collapsed before they could even scream. A merchant in the market square was suddenly aged decades in a second, turning to dust before his eyes.
"Look at what you’re doing, Theo," Rex crooned, his voice echoing inside. Theo’s mind is like a poisonous hallucination. "Your power is hungry... It’s eating your people."
Theo’s eyes flew open, blood streaming from them. "No... I didn’t... I’m not doing this!"
"STOP IT!" But his voice was drowned out by the psychic feedback Rex was feeding him.
"Let’s show them the truth," Rex decided. His eyes burned with a malevolent silver light. "Let’s give them a show they’ll never forget."
Rex seized the core of Theo’s temporal magic and performed a grand temporal rewind, but he didn’t rewind the world; he rewound the perception of the world.
He created a massive, sky-spanning projection, a temporal mirror that forced the entire city to relive the last hour through Theo’s eyes.
KRA KOOOOOM!
The sky above Aethelgard split open. A massive, shimmering curtain of golden light descended over the city.
Everyone... every citizen, every guard, every noble stopped in their tracks, their necks craning upward.
And there, in the sky, they saw it.

They saw the visions of the slaughter Rex had orchestrated, but Rex had framed it perfectly. Through the temporal projection, it didn’t look like Rex was killing innocents; it looked like Theo was deliberately unleashing his rage upon them, his face twisted in demonic glee as he tore through the populace.
’WAAAAAHHHH!’ The screams of the projected victims echoed across the city.
Aurelia saw it.
"My son..." she gasped, her voice breaking. "What have you become?"
Beside her, the ancient eyes of Morwenna narrowed. She saw through the magical distortion, but the emotional weight of the image was undeniable.
The sin was laid bare before the gods.
"The bloodline is tainted," Morwenna whispered, her voice cold as winter. "The boy has invited darkness that cannot be undone."
