chapters.title: Chapter 1058. A Disgraced Prince Running From a Shadow
paragraphs: Rex turned back to the convulsing Theo, who was weeping in agony as he felt his mother’s horror through their psychic connection.
"See that?" Rex asked, tilting his head as he watched the city descend into panic. "That’s the sound of your world breaking."
"You wanted to be a god of time, Theo."
"Now, you’re just the monster that time will forget."
Rex’s fingers tightened around Theo’s magical core. The clash wasn’t physical anymore; it was a war of narrative and soul.
Rex was rewriting Theo’s history in real time, using the very magic Theo had used to try and kill him.
"Now," Rex said, his voice dropping to a deadly whisper as he prepared to unleash the final blow of manipulation. "Let’s see how much more you can take before you beg me to kill you."
High above the dimensional veil, in a realm where time flowed like molten gold, Kaeleth watched the unfolding catastrophe with a cold, detached fury.
For the first time in eons, the Primordial Entity felt something akin to disgust. He had placed his hopes in an apostle, a vessel meant to channel his divine wrath, and he had chosen Theo.
"Pathetic," Kaeleth’s voice rumbled through the void, each syllable vibrating with cosmic disappointment. "A broken instrument."
"A child playing with lightning who has now burned down his own house."
Kaeleth withdrew his divine gaze, severing the connection. He knew that continuing to watch would only feed Theo’s desperation.
If Rex truly intended to breach the Primordial Domain, Kaeleth needed to stop being a spectator and start being a strategist. The apostle was a lost cause; the pawn had become a liability.
Down in the courtyard, the psychological slaughter was reaching its crescendo.
Theo was drowning. It wasn’t just the physical pain anymore; it was the psychic assault of a thousand voices.
Through Rex’s manipulation of his senses, Theo could hear every whisper, every scream, and every curse echoing from the streets of Aethelgard.
"Kill him! End the monster!"
"Rex, please! Save us from his madness!"
"He’s not one of us anymore; he’s a demon!"
"No... no, no, no!" Theo shrieked, clawing at his own ears, but the voices were inside his skull. "I didn’t do it!"
"Rex, stop it! I’m innocent! I’m innocent!"

Rex let out a theatrical sigh, one that carried across the temporal projection to every citizen in the city. He moved to stand protectively in front of the weeping Theo, putting his back to the boy as if shielding the city from Theo’s very presence.
"I’m trying, citizens of Aethelgard!" Rex shouted toward the sky, his voice amplified by temporal harmonics so it sounded like thunder. "I am trying to contain his rage!"
"I am trying to hold back the tide of his corruption, but his power is too volatile! He cannot control himself!"
It was the perfect lie. By pretending to restrain Theo, Rex was framing Theo’s desperate pleas as the incoherent ramblings of a madman.
"Mother! Morwenna!" Theo screamed, looking toward the palace. "Please, you have to believe me! I didn’t kill them!"
But Aurelia didn’t look at him with love. Her eyes were hollow, filled with a grief so profound it had turned into revulsion.
"My son is dead," she whispered, tears streaming down her face. "There is only this... this thing wearing his skin."
Morwenna’s ancient face was a mask of granite. "The corruption has taken root.
"Mercy would be a sin against the ancestors."
Then came Valentina. Her voice pierced through the chaos like a blade.
"REX!" she screamed, her face contorted with terror and rage. "DO NOT LET HIM BREATHE ANOTHER SECOND! "
"END THIS MADNESS NOW! KILL HIM BEFORE HE ERASES US ALL!"
Theo’s heart shattered. The betrayal was worse than any blade Rex could wield.
"Headmaster Valentina? No... you too?"
Rex turned his head slightly, offering Theo a smile that was nothing short of demonic. "Hear that, Theo?"
"Even your allies have seen the truth. Even your blood has condemned you."
Rex’s hands began to glow with a soft, deceptive blue light the color of ’purification.’ He leaned down to Theo’s ear one last time, whispering so low only the boy could hear.
"I’m not framing you, Theo."
"I’m simply revealing what everyone already knows: that you are a failure."
Rex stood up straight, turning to face the sky, his arms spread wide as if accepting the burden of a tragic hero.
"Forgive me, Aethelgard," Rex cried out, his voice dripping with false solemnity. "But for the safety of all, the monster must fall!"

As Rex raised his hand to deliver what looked like a merciful execution, Theo could only stare up at the sky with empty, broken eyes. He had lost everything: his power, his people, his family, and his soul.
He was no longer a threat; he was merely a victim of a narrative he could no longer fight.
The world stopped.

Not the gradual slowing of time that Theo was used to, but an absolute, violent cessation of motion. The falling debris from the courtyard was frozen midair; the distant screams of the panicked citizens were severed midnote, leaving a silence so heavy it felt like being buried alive.
Rex had seized control of the temporal flow entirely, locking the entire dimension into a static photograph where only he and Theo could move.

Rex walked through the frozen battlefield with lazy confidence, stepping over suspended droplets of blood as if they were pebbles on a path. He approached Theo, who was suspended in a state of perpetual panic, his muscles locked in a futile attempt to flee.
"This is it, Theo," Rex said, his voice echoing unnaturally in the frozen void. "The final act."
"No more magic... No more grand speeches about destiny."
"Since your soul couldn’t handle the truth, I’m going to break you from the outside."
Rex grabbed Theo’s chin, forcing him to look into those cold, silver eyes. "I’ve dismantled your reputation."
"I’ve dismantled your family’s love."
"I’ve made you a ghost in your own kingdom." Rex leaned in closer, his smile widening into something truly grotesque. "And here’s the best part: Aurelia is already grieving you."
"And soon, she will find comfort in someone else."
"Someone stronger. Someone who isn’t a fraud. A new heir will be born, Theo!
"A real son. One who won’t embarrass the bloodline."
Something snapped inside Theo. The despair didn’t vanish; it curdled.
It turned into a poisonous, acidic rage that had no outlet because he couldn’t even move his arms to strike. The humiliation was too vast, too intimate.
"You... you fucking piece of shit!" Theo’s voice tore through the frozen air, cracking with venom. "You think this matters?! You think I care about a throne built on lies?"
Rex raised an eyebrow, amused. "Oh? The mouse has teeth?"
"You think you’ve won?" Theo spat, tears of rage streaming down his face. "You’re nothing but a parasite, Rex! "
"You think you’re some mastermind?!"
"You’re just a filthy dog who couldn’t take what he wanted honestly, so you fucked your way through my life!"

"You fucked Diana when she wasn’t looking, you crawled into my aunt’s bed, you touched my grandmother’s skin like some diseased animal, and you even crawled under my mother’s skirts while she wept for me!"
Theo’s insults became a torrent of profanity, a desperate attempt to wound the unassailable Rex. "You’re a fucking piece of shit, Rex!"
"A cosmic dick who feeds on the scraps of better women! You didn’t win; you just stole what you couldn’t earn!"
Rex didn’t flinch. He didn’t even look angry.
He simply watched Theo’s face with the detached interest of a scientist watching a bug squirm in alcohol.
"Is that all?" Rex asked quietly. "All that anger, and you’re still just shouting at a god."
Rex’s grip tightened, and suddenly, he released the temporal lock but not for everyone. He released it only for Theo’s legs while keeping his upper body sluggish and heavy.
"Run, little mouse," Rex whispered. "Run while you still have legs to carry your shame."
The sudden return of physics hit Theo like a physical blow. The weight of his own guilt, the horror of what his family now believed, and the sheer terror of Rex’s presence overwhelmed him.
The bravado, the insults—they all evaporated instantly, leaving behind nothing but a terrified, broken child.
"No... stay away from me!" Theo shrieked. His legs moved instinctively, not in a combat stance, but in a desperate, clumsy sprint.
He turned and bolted. He didn’t fight back.
He didn’t try to summon a single spark of Kaeleth’s power. He ran like a coward, his boots skidding on the cobblestones as he fled toward the city gates, sobbing hysterically.
His cape fluttered behind him like the broken wings of a fallen bird.
Rex stood in the center of the courtyard, watching the retreating figure. He didn’t give chase.
He didn’t need to. He had already won.
He watched as Theo disappeared into the maze of Aethelgard, a disgraced prince running from a shadow he could never outpace.
Rex turned back to the frozen world, a satisfied hum vibrating in his chest.
"Now," he mused, looking at the frozen face of Aurelia in the distance. "Let’s see what else I can break."

chapters.title: Chapter 1059. Today, You Will Simply Bleed
paragraphs: Rex didn’t run; he glided. He moved through the streets of Aethelgard like a predator through tall grass, the temporal distortion around him making his approach silent and unnerving.

Theo was a mess of panicked motion; one moment he was sprinting down an alleyway, boots pounding against stone, the next he was desperately taking to the air, his wings of golden light flickering erratically as he tried to escape the gravity of his own failure.
"Running won’t change the ending, Theo!" Rex’s voice boomed, not from his mouth, but from the very air around Theo’s ears. "You can fly to the heavens, but I own the space between the stars!"
WHOOSH BOOM!
Without warning, Rex snapped his fingers. A lance of concentrated cryo magic materialized midair behind Theo, streaking forward like a comet.
Theo twisted his body in mid-flight, the ice grazing his ribs with a sound like shattering glass CRACKLE and leaving a trail of frost that burned his skin.
"Fuck you! Stay away!" Theo screamed, his voice cracking as he pushed his flight to its absolute limit, leaving a trail of golden sparks behind him.
Rex’s eyes gleamed. "Too slow."
Rex raised both hands, weaving his fingers through the air as if playing an invisible harp. Telekinetic Force slammed into Theo’s back like a battering ram.
THUD.
The boy was hurled downward, crashing through the thatched roof of a tavern.
CRUNCH.

Before Theo could even scramble out of the debris, Rex unleashed a barrage of elemental fury. From his fingertips shot three distinct streams: a spiraling vortex of pyromancy, a jagged bolt of lightning, and a crushing wave of gravitational pressure.
FWOOOOSH ZAP KRA KOOOOM!

Theo screamed as the fire singed his hair, the lightning arced across his nervous system, making his muscles spasm uncontrollably, and the gravity pinned him to the broken floorboards. He lay there, gasping, blood bubbling at the corner of his mouth.
"Get up," Rex commanded, walking leisurely into the ruined tavern.
The wooden planks groaned under his weight. "I haven’t even started the real lesson."
Theo tried to summon a shield, his hands shaking as he attempted to channel Kaeleth’s power. A weak, translucent barrier flickered into existence.
Vrrrrm.
Rex didn’t even flinch. He simply extended a palm. "Let’s see how your ’divine’ protection holds up against raw entropy."
Rex unleashed a Void Pulse. A sphere of pure black energy erupted from his palm.
When it hit Theo’s shield, there was no explosion, only a sickening sound of something being erased.
Ssssssssss.
The shield didn’t break; it simply ceased to exist, and the void energy tore through Theo’s shoulder, sending him spinning across the floor.
"Why won’t you die?!" Theo wailed, crawling backward on his elbows, his eyes bloodshot and wild. "Just kill me and be done with it!"
"Because death is too merciful for a coward like you," Rex sneered.
He raised his hand again, and this time, the air itself seemed to crystallize. "I want you to feel every second of your inadequacy."
Rex began a complex series of hand seals. The air temperature plummeted while simultaneously igniting with static.

He launched a Chain Lightning Storm fused with Magma Cores. The attack came in waves. First the lightning struck, paralyzing Theo’s limbs BZZZZZT, and then the molten projectiles followed, exploding against his flesh like miniature grenades.
KABOOM. KABOOM.

Theo was tossed around like a ragdoll in a hurricane. He tried to fly again, desperate to reach the sky, but Rex used Telekinetic Snare, invisible tendrils of force wrapping around Theo’s ankles and wrists.
YANK.
Theo was jerked back down to earth, his body slamming into the cobblestone street with a wet THWACK.
Rex stood over him, the shadows stretching unnaturally long.
"Look at you," Rex said, tilting his head as he watched Theo convulse in pain. "The Apostle of the Time."
"Those who said that you’re going to be the savior of Aethelgard... but in reality... you’re just a broken, sobbing wreck bleeding in the dirt."
Rex’s hands began to glow with a sickly purple light, Soul Crushing Gravity. The pressure increased exponentially.
The cobblestones beneath Theo began to crack and spiderweb.
CRACK CRACK CRACK.

"This is the choreography of your defeat, Theo," Rex whispered as he increased the power, watching as Theo’s bones began to creak under the magical weight. "Every strike, every element, every ounce of pain... it’s all designed to remind you that you never belonged here."
The cobblestones beneath Theo were no longer stone; they had been ground into fine powder by the sheer pressure of Rex’s magical presence.
Theo lay in the center of a crater, his breathing coming in ragged, wet gasps. His ribs were shattered, his vision was swimming in crimson, and every nerve ending screamed in agony.
Just as his eyes began to roll back, just as the sweet darkness of unconsciousness promised an end to the pain, Rex intervened.
"Not yet, little mouse," Rex whispered. "We haven’t reached the climax."
Rex raised his hand, and a sickly green glow erupted from his palm.
"Supreme Healing."
Theo’s body convulsed violently.
SQUELCH.
The sound of bones knitting back together was nauseating, like wet wood snapping. Skin fused over open wounds with an agonizing heat that felt like molten lead being poured into his veins.
The pain of healing was worse than the pain of the wounds themselves; it was an invasive, violating sensation that forced his consciousness back to the surface with brutal efficiency.
"Nnngh... ah... HAAAAAH!" Theo screamed as his lungs inflated painfully.
His heart hammered against his chest like a trapped bird. "Stop... please... just kill me..."
"Kill you?" Rex laughed, a cold, melodic sound that cut through the ringing in Theo’s ears. "You had a second chance, Theo."
"When Kaeleth gave you that spark, when you stood there thinking you could challenge the inevitable, you wasted it."
"You thought you could fight me with borrowed divinity? The result was always going to be this: you, bleeding in the dirt, while I stand above you."
Rex moved with terrifying fluidity. He didn’t just attack; he performed a symphony of cruelty. He raised his left hand, conjuring a blade of Pure Plasma.
With a flick of his wrist, he sent a crescent wave of superheated energy slicing through the air.
SHIIIIIIING.
Theo scrambled to his feet, his legs still unsteady from the forced healing. He threw up a desperate Light Shield, but Rex’s plasma cut through it like a hot knife through butter.
The energy sliced across Theo’s chest, reopening the wounds that had just healed, sending blood spraying across the crater.
SPLAT.
"KAELETH! "Theo shrieked toward the heavens, his voice breaking into a raw, guttural howl. "KAELETH, HELP ME! I’M SORRY!
"PLEASE, I’LL DO ANYTHING! JUST MAKE HIM STOP!"
The sky remained silent. The golden clouds of Aethelgard didn’t part; the divine light didn’t descend.
There was only the indifferent wind and the mocking echo of his own desperation.
"He’s not coming, Theo," Rex said, stepping closer, his boots clicking against the stone. "He’s already moved on."
"To him, you’re just a broken toy. And I? I’m the one who gets to play with the pieces."
Rex’s hands began to move in complex, overlapping patterns. Elemental Convergence.
The air around him began to warp and bend. Suddenly, he unleashed a storm of shattered glass—thousands of razor-sharp shards of crystallized mana, each imbued with lightning and frost.
K K K K SHHHHHHHH!
The shards rained down in a deadly spiral. Theo tried to dodge, but Rex used Telekinetic Guidance to steer the shards mid-flight.
Each crystal found a mark. One pierced his thigh, another his shoulder, and another grazed his cheek.
THWIP. THWIP. CRUNCH.
Theo fell to his knees, the magical shards embedded in his flesh glowing with malevolent energy.
"Please... no more..." Theo sobbed, blood streaming down his chin.
"No more?" Rex’s eyes flared with silver light. "We’re just getting to the best part."
Rex clenched his fist. Gravitational Collapse.
A localized field of intense gravity slammed down directly onto Theo’s shoulders.
BOOOOOM.
The impact forced Theo face-first into the rubble. As Theo struggled to lift his head, Rex unleashed a continuous stream of corrosive acidic fire.
FSSSSSSSSSSSS.

The flames didn’t just burn; they ate. They hissed as they touched Theo’s flesh, turning skin to blackened char. Theo’s screams became inhuman, a continuous stream of agony that seemed to vibrate the very foundations of the city.
He tried to summon one last burst of power, a desperate solar flare, to blind Rex.
VROOOOOOM.
The flash was brilliant, but Rex simply walked through it, his eyes unblinking. He caught Theo by the hair, yanking his head back to expose his throat.
"Look at me, Theo," Rex commanded, his voice dropping to a deadly whisper. "Look at the man who took everything."
"Your power, your family, your dignity... Tomorrow, they will forget you ever existed."
"Today, you will simply bleed."
Rex raised his other hand, gathering a sphere of Void Energy that hummed with the sound of a thousand dying stars.
HUMMMMMMM.

His ribs were shattered, his vision was swimming in crimson, and every nerve ending screamed in agony.
Just as his eyes began to roll back, just as the sweet darkness of unconsciousness promised an end to the pain, Rex intervened.
"Not yet, little mouse," Rex whispered.
"We haven’t reached the climax."
Rex raised his hand, and a sickly green glow erupted from his palm.
"Supreme Healing."
Theo’s body convulsed violently.
SQUELCH.
The sound of bones knitting back together was nauseating, like wet wood snapping.
Skin fused over open wounds with an agonizing heat that felt like molten lead being poured into his veins.
The pain of healing was worse than the pain of the wounds themselves; it was an invasive, violating sensation that forced his consciousness back to the surface with brutal efficiency.
"Nnngh... ah...
HAAAAAH!" Theo screamed as his lungs inflated painfully.
His heart hammered against his chest like a trapped bird.
"Stop... please... just kill me..."
"Kill you?" Rex laughed, a cold, melodic sound that cut through the ringing in Theo’s ears.
"You had a second chance, Theo."
"When Kaeleth gave you that spark, when you stood there thinking you could challenge the inevitable, you wasted it."
"You thought you could fight me with borrowed divinity?
The result was always going to be this: you, bleeding in the dirt, while I stand above you."
Rex moved with terrifying fluidity.
He didn’t just attack; he performed a symphony of cruelty.
He raised his left hand, conjuring a blade of Pure Plasma.
With a flick of his wrist, he sent a crescent wave of superheated energy slicing through the air.
SHIIIIIIING.
Theo scrambled to his feet, his legs still unsteady from the forced healing.
He threw up a desperate Light Shield, but Rex’s plasma cut through it like a hot knife through butter.
The energy sliced across Theo’s chest, reopening the wounds that had just healed, sending blood spraying across the crater.
SPLAT.
"KAELETH!
"Theo shrieked toward the heavens, his voice breaking into a raw, guttural howl.
"KAELETH, HELP ME!
I’M SORRY!
"PLEASE, I’LL DO ANYTHING!
JUST MAKE HIM STOP!"
The sky remained silent.
The golden clouds of Aethelgard didn’t part; the divine light didn’t descend.
There was only the indifferent wind and the mocking echo of his own desperation.
"He’s not coming, Theo," Rex said, stepping closer, his boots clicking against the stone.
"He’s already moved on."
"To him, you’re just a broken toy.
And I?
I’m the one who gets to play with the pieces."
Rex’s hands began to move in complex, overlapping patterns.
Elemental Convergence.
The air around him began to warp and bend.
Suddenly, he unleashed a storm of shattered glass—thousands of razor-sharp shards of crystallized mana, each imbued with lightning and frost.
K K K K SHHHHHHHH!
The shards rained down in a deadly spiral.
Theo tried to dodge, but Rex used Telekinetic Guidance to steer the shards mid-flight.
Each crystal found a mark.
One pierced his thigh, another his shoulder, and another grazed his cheek.
THWIP.
THWIP.
CRUNCH.
Theo fell to his knees, the magical shards embedded in his flesh glowing with malevolent energy.
"Please... no more..." Theo sobbed, blood streaming down his chin.
"No more?" Rex’s eyes flared with silver light.
"We’re just getting to the best part."
Rex clenched his fist.
Gravitational Collapse.
A localized field of intense gravity slammed down directly onto Theo’s shoulders.
BOOOOOM.
The impact forced Theo face-first into the rubble.
As Theo struggled to lift his head, Rex unleashed a continuous stream of corrosive acidic fire.
FSSSSSSSSSSSS.
The flames didn’t just burn; they ate.
They hissed as they touched Theo’s flesh, turning skin to blackened char.
Theo’s screams became inhuman, a continuous stream of agony that seemed to vibrate the very foundations of the city.
He tried to summon one last burst of power, a desperate solar flare, to blind Rex.
VROOOOOOM.
The flash was brilliant, but Rex simply walked through it, his eyes unblinking.
He caught Theo by the hair, yanking his head back to expose his throat.
"Look at me, Theo," Rex commanded, his voice dropping to a deadly whisper.
"Look at the man who took everything."
"Your power, your family, your dignity...
Tomorrow, they will forget you ever existed."
"Today, you will simply bleed."
Rex raised his other hand, gathering a sphere of Void Energy that hummed with the sound of a thousand dying stars.
HUMMMMMMM.

chapters.title: Chapter 1060. A Hollow Man Walking Toward a Future He No Longer Believed In
paragraphs: Rex extended his right hand, palm upward. The gesture was almost tender, a mockery of comfort offered to a dying man.
His fingers didn’t twitch; they remained perfectly still, suspended in the charged, blood-soaked air of the crater.
Theo stared at that hand. His vision was a fractured mosaic of crimson tears and golden sparks.
His mind was a screaming void, a cacophony of agony that refused to subside. ’Why is he doing this?’
’Why isn’t it over?’ Theo thought, his consciousness flickering like a candle in a hurricane. ’I can’t feel my legs.’
’I can’t feel my ribs.’
’I can’t even feel my own god anymore.’
’Kaeleth... where are you? Why is it so cold?’
The silence between them was heavier than the gravity Rex had been wielding. It was the silence of a predator waiting for its prey to finally accept its fate.

With a wet, shuddering gasp that sounded like tearing parchment, Theo reached out. His fingers, slick with his own warm blood and blackened by magical burns, trembled violently as they moved through the air.
When his palm finally met Rex’s, the contact was obscene—the touch of a broken animal against the cold silk of a god.
Then, the extraction began.
It wasn’t the thunderous roar of a spell or the explosive force of a physical blow. There was no flash of light, no dramatic shockwave that would shake the foundations of Aethelgard.
Instead, it was something far more terrifying: a surgical, intimate violation.
Rex’s Soul Manipulation began its work. It was a quiet process, possessing the unnerving, professional stillness of an undertaker removing a cherished trinket from a corpse.

The magic threaded itself into Theo’s very essence, finding the precise geometric coordinates where the Temporal Designation, the divine authority granted by Kaeleth, was woven into his spiritual architecture.
Theo’s breath hitched. His pupils dilated until his eyes were nothing but black pits of terror.
’It’s not pain,’ Theo realized with a horrifying clarity. ’It’s... emptiness.’

It felt as though a fundamental part of his identity was being unmade. Imagine a limb being severed, but without the nerves screaming, just the sudden, impossible awareness of a missing space where something vital used to be.

The ’negative volume’ of his divinity left a hollow cavity in his soul, a spiritual wound that could never be closed by flesh knitting magic. The authority that had made him a prince, a warrior, a chosen one, was being peeled away like skin from muscle.
’I am nothing,’ Theo’s inner voice whimpered, fading into the static of his trauma. ’I am a hollow shell.’
’There is nothing left inside me but the dark.’

Rex’s expression remained impassive as he felt the designation slip into his grasp. He could sense the exact dimensional address of the authority; he had just stolen the specific coordinates in the multiverse where Kaeleth’s domain resided, now exposed and vulnerable through the stolen key.
[SYSTEM NOTIFICATION]
[Temporal Designation Navigation Component Integrated.]
[Dimensional Manipulation + Temporal Navigation: Kaeleth’s Domain Location Confirmed.]
The data flooded Rex’s consciousness with flawless clarity. The map of the divine was laid bare before him.
The fortress of the god was no longer an unreachable sanctuary; it was now a target with a confirmed address.
Rex’s fingers curled around the stolen essence, securing it. The transaction was complete.
The prince was no longer a prince; he was merely a broken body waiting to be discarded.
Rex released Theo’s hand.
The courtyard was no longer a place of beauty; it was a slaughterhouse floor, slick with the arterial spray that painted the ancient stones crimson.

Theo stood swaying in the center of the carnage, his body a roadmap of trauma: blackened flesh, exposed bone fragments peeking through torn muscle, and the raw, weeping wounds where Rex’s magic had repeatedly flayed him open only to stitch him back together for more pain.
But the physical agony was now secondary to the spiritual void. Theo stared at his hands.
They were shaking so violently they looked blurred, stained dark with blood that refused to dry. He felt lighter, but it was the lightness of a gutted fish, of something hollowed out and left to rot.
"Is it... gone?" Theo whispered.
His voice was a broken rasp, stripped raw from hours of screaming. He wasn’t asking about the pain.
He was asking about the emptiness.
Rex stood before him, untouched by the chaos he had orchestrated. His eyes held the cold satisfaction of a craftsman who had just finished a delicate extraction.
"Yes," Rex said, the word landing with the finality of a guillotine blade. "The designation is mine..."
"The connection is severed. You are utterly, magnificently alone."
Theo looked at his hands for a moment longer. A single tear tracked through the grime and blood on his cheek, leaving a pale streak.
"Good," he said.
The word was hollow, devoid of hope, carrying only the acceptance of a man who had seen the bottom of hell and decided to make a home there.
Rex’s gaze sharpened, studying the wreckage of the boy before him.
"Go inside," Rex commanded, his voice dropping to a tone of warning. "Retreat to the household."
"Lock the doors. The next portion of this... the next phase of what comes next... is not something you want to be adjacent to."
Theo lifted his head. His eyes were bloodshot, sunken into bruised sockets, but they burned with a terrible, lucid understanding.

He looked at Rex with an expression that defied simple categorization; it was the look of a traitor who had betrayed himself, the complicated grief of someone who had just handed the keys to his own executioner.
"You are going to kill him," Theo said.
It wasn’t a question; it was a diagnosis of the inevitable.
"Yes," Rex replied without hesitation.
"Kaeleth," Theo breathed, the name of his god tasting like ash in his mouth.
"Yes."
A heavy, suffocating silence descended upon the courtyard. The only sounds were the distant crackle of magical residue and Theo’s own wet, labored breathing.
Inside his mind, Theo was drowning in a sea of regret.
’I thought I was the hero of this story,’ he thought bitterly. ’I thought I was the chosen vessel. ’
’But I was just the bait. I was the delivery system for my own god’s downfall.’
"He gave me a second chance," Theo said aloud, his voice cracking. "That’s what he told me."
"When the light came back, when he mended my bones and gave me the power to stand against you again... he told me it was mercy."
"A second chance to make things right."
Rex took a step forward, his shadow swallowing Theo’s broken form. "He didn’t give you mercy, Theo."
"He gave you a weapon. He pointed it at me, knowing exactly how you would react."
"The ’second chance’ was nothing more than a psychological framing, a lie wrapped in golden light to make you willing to be the arrow in his quiver."
Theo closed his eyes. The image of Kaeleth’s radiant face flashed in his mind, now twisted by the realization of its true intent.
"I know," Theo whispered. "I knew it."
"Somewhere, deep beneath the terror and the pain, I knew."
"I just couldn’t find the ’somewhere’ until you tore it out of me."
Rex stared at him for a long beat, seeing nothing left to break. The boy was already shattered beyond repair.
"Go inside," Rex repeated, the command brooks no argument. "Before I decide you’re still worth the effort of breaking further."
Theo didn’t fight. He didn’t weep.
He simply turned, each step a monumental struggle against gravity and agony, and limped toward the safety of the house, a hollow man walking toward a future he no longer believed in.

chapters.title: Chapter 1061. A Perpetual Moment of Maximum Agony
paragraphs: Rex stood alone in the courtyard, the silence of the aftermath settling like ash over the blood-soaked stones. He watched Theo’s retreating figure stumble toward the house, a broken, hollowed-out shell of a man.
A cruel, razor-sharp smile tugged at the corner of Rex’s mouth.
"Did you really think I was done?" Rex whispered to the empty air. "Did you truly believe I would let you walk away with such... incomplete satisfaction?"
With a casual flick of his wrist, Rex activated Telekinetic Suspension. An invisible, crushing force seized Theo mid-step.
The boy’s body jerked violently upward, his spine snapping taut as he was yanked off the ground and suspended ten feet in the air.
"Nngh AHHHH!" Theo’s scream was cut short as the telekinetic grip tightened around his torso like a vice.
CRACK.
His ribs groaned under the pressure.
"You want to leave?" Rex’s voice carried across the courtyard, cold and amused. "You haven’t earned your exit yet."

Rex raised both hands, his fingers weaving through the air as if plucking invisible strings. He wasn’t just using telekinesis; he was layering it with something far more insidious: temporal loop torture.
The telekinetic force began to work with mechanical cruelty. It didn’t just hold Theo; it began to twist.
The invisible hands grabbed Theo’s limbs and pulled in opposing directions.
SQUELCH. SNAP.

His shoulder dislocated with a wet pop, then his elbow followed. But as soon as the pain reached its crescendo, as soon as Theo’s eyes rolled back and his heart began to flutter toward failure, Rex activated the Chrono Rewind.
VROOOOOM WHIP.
Time stuttered. The blood that had sprayed across the stones flew backward into the wounds; the bones that had shattered fused back together in a reverse cascade of agony.
Theo’s body was yanked back to its state moments before the injury.
"No... no please... NO!" Theo shrieked, his voice cracking into a high-pitched, pathetic wail. "STOP IT! STOP IT!"
"Let’s try this angle instead," Rex mused.
The telekinetic grip shifted. This time, it focused on Theo’s ribcage, crushing inward with increasing pressure.
CRUNCH. CRUNCH.
The sound of breaking bone was constant, a rhythmic percussion of suffering. Theo’s lungs collapsed, his mouth opening in a silent scream before the blood flooded his throat.
Just as his vision faded into the blackness of death, WHIP.
Time rewound again.
"Again," Rex commanded.

The cycle became a hellish loop of impossible physics. Rex would use telekinesis to tear Theo apart, ripping muscle from bone and flaying skin from flesh in slow motion, and then, with a flick of his fingers, rewind the clock.
Theo was trapped in a perpetual moment of maximum agony, a human marionette caught in a glitch of reality.
SHRED. SNAP. WHIP.
SHRED. SNAP. WHIP.
Theo’s screams had long since lost their human quality. They were primal, animalistic shrieks of pure, unadulterated terror.

He was screaming like a bitch, his voice reduced to a raw, grating noise that tore at his own vocal cords. His mind was fracturing; the constant rewinding meant he never received the mercy of unconsciousness.
He was forced to experience every millisecond of his own destruction over and over, his consciousness forcibly reassembled along with his flesh.
’I’m dying... I’m dying... I’m dying...’ Theo’s inner thoughts screamed in terror, only to be reset. ’I’m dying... I’m dying...’

Rex watched the display with the rapt attention of an artist watching paint dry. He watched the way the blood spiraled backward, the way the light caught the wetness of Theo’s exposed organs before they were pulled back inside, the way the boy’s face contorted in a mask of eternal horror.

The courtyard became a stage for a god of cruelty. The air hummed with the static of broken time, the only sound the wet tearing of flesh and the endless, broken sobbing of a man who had discovered that even death was not an escape from Rex.
After what felt like hours of exquisite torment, Rex finally ceased the spell. The telekinetic grip vanished, dropping Theo’s limp, convulsing body to the stones like a sack of meat.
Theo lay there, twitching spasmodically, his mind shattered into a thousand screaming fragments, unable to even comprehend that the pain had stopped.
Rex stood over him, the moonlight catching the silver in his eyes. He didn’t feel pity; he felt exhilarated.
The power to control not just life and death, but the very sequence of suffering itself, was intoxicating.
A low chuckle rumbled in Rex’s chest, building into a full, unrestrained peal of laughter that echoed off the walls of the courtyard, mocking the broken boy bleeding in the dirt.

Rex stood amidst the carnage, the silence of the courtyard now a canvas for his cold, calculating mind. He didn’t just see the world; he processed it as a series of variables to be manipulated, exploited, and conquered.
Within his dimensional awareness, he could feel the stolen prize. The Temporal Designation’s navigation component hummed with a foreign, divine energy.

It wasn’t just data; it was a living pulse. He could sense the specific dimensional address of Kaeleth’s domain, the exact metaphysical coordinates of a god’s sanctuary, sitting nestled within his Dimensional Manipulation like a poisoned needle on a map.
It was precise.
It was accessible.
It was his.
’Almost there,’ Rex thought, a predator’s satisfaction coiling in his gut. ’I have the key to the kingdom, and the gates don’t even know I’m coming.’
He checked his internal systems with clinical detachment. His Presence Manipulation was operating at a perfect baseline signature compression.
His divine class aura, the kind of power that would normally set off every alarm in the celestial heavens, was crushed down, folded, and hidden beneath the mundane, pathetic profile of a mortal.
He was a wolf wearing the skin of a lamb, invisible to Kaeleth’s defensive architecture. He would walk through the god’s front door before the first warning bell could even ring.

His mind swept through the extensive coverage list of Full Potential Adaptation. His consciousness catalogued every temporal working class, every divine expression, and every magical mechanism that Theo’s stolen designation had ever produced.

He had learned from every wound he had inflicted on the boy; he had adapted to every defense Theo had attempted to mount. He wasn’t just fighting a god; he was fighting a god with the experience of every mortal who had ever dared to defy him.
For a fleeting second, a different image surfaced in the darkness of his mind. He thought of Aurelia.
He thought of the child she was carrying, the fragile, growing heartbeat that represented something beyond mere conquest. But Rex’s thoughts weren’t tender; they were possessive and strategic.
He thought about how that child would grow up in a Nightwing household that would be fundamentally different from the one Theo had known. This wasn’t about sentimentality; it was about legacy.
The last month of brutal, unforgiving training had forged the Nightwing unit into something else entirely: a weaponized fighting force held to a standard of absolute efficiency.
They would become a machine that would continue to function long after Rex had ascended or moved on. They would be his living monument.
He took that thought, that flicker of future planning, and filed it away in the cold compartment of his mind reserved for his lasting constructs.
He compartmentalized his humanity, his legacy, and his attachments with the same ruthless precision he used to dismantle Theo’s soul.
Then, he shut that door. He killed the thought.
The next hour required no legacy. It required no future, and it required no mercy.
The next hour was not for building; it was for breaking. The next hour was not for thinking about what would continue.
The next hour belonged to Kaeleth.

The telekinetic grip vanished, dropping Theo’s limp, convulsing body to the stones like a sack of meat.
Theo lay there, twitching spasmodically, his mind shattered into a thousand screaming fragments, unable to even comprehend that the pain had stopped.
Rex stood over him, the moonlight catching the silver in his eyes.
He didn’t feel pity; he felt exhilarated.
The power to control not just life and death, but the very sequence of suffering itself, was intoxicating.
A low chuckle rumbled in Rex’s chest, building into a full, unrestrained peal of laughter that echoed off the walls of the courtyard, mocking the broken boy bleeding in the dirt.
Rex stood amidst the carnage, the silence of the courtyard now a canvas for his cold, calculating mind.
He didn’t just see the world; he processed it as a series of variables to be manipulated, exploited, and conquered.
Within his dimensional awareness, he could feel the stolen prize.
The Temporal Designation’s navigation component hummed with a foreign, divine energy.
It wasn’t just data; it was a living pulse.

He could sense the specific dimensional address of Kaeleth’s domain, the exact metaphysical coordinates of a god’s sanctuary, sitting nestled within his Dimensional Manipulation like a poisoned needle on a map.
It was precise.
It was accessible.
It was his.
’Almost there,’ Rex thought, a predator’s satisfaction coiling in his gut. ’I have the key to the kingdom, and the gates don’t even know I’m coming.’
He checked his internal systems with clinical detachment.
His Presence Manipulation was operating at a perfect baseline signature compression.
His divine class aura, the kind of power that would normally set off every alarm in the celestial heavens, was crushed down, folded, and hidden beneath the mundane, pathetic profile of a mortal.
He was a wolf wearing the skin of a lamb, invisible to Kaeleth’s defensive architecture.
He would walk through the god’s front door before the first warning bell could even ring.
His mind swept through the extensive coverage list of Full Potential Adaptation.
His consciousness catalogued every temporal working class, every divine expression, and every magical mechanism that Theo’s stolen designation had ever produced.
He had learned from every wound he had inflicted on the boy; he had adapted to every defense Theo had attempted to mount.
He wasn’t just fighting a god; he was fighting a god with the experience of every mortal who had ever dared to defy him.
For a fleeting second, a different image surfaced in the darkness of his mind.
He thought of Aurelia.
He thought of the child she was carrying, the fragile, growing heartbeat that represented something beyond mere conquest.
But Rex’s thoughts weren’t tender; they were possessive and strategic.
He thought about how that child would grow up in a Nightwing household that would be fundamentally different from the one Theo had known.
This wasn’t about sentimentality; it was about legacy.
The last month of brutal, unforgiving training had forged the Nightwing unit into something else entirely: a weaponized fighting force held to a standard of absolute efficiency.
They would become a machine that would continue to function long after Rex had ascended or moved on.
They would be his living monument.
He took that thought, that flicker of future planning, and filed it away in the cold compartment of his mind reserved for his lasting constructs.
He compartmentalized his humanity, his legacy, and his attachments with the same ruthless precision he used to dismantle Theo’s soul.
Then, he shut that door.
He killed the thought.
The next hour required no legacy.
It required no future, and it required no mercy.
The next hour was not for building; it was for breaking.
The next hour was not for thinking about what would continue.
The next hour belonged to Kaeleth.

chapters.title: Chapter 1062. A Thought Made Manifest Through Absolute Violence
paragraphs: Rex initiated the sequence with the clinical detachment of a surgeon cutting into living tissue. Temporal Stop.
The world didn’t just freeze; it died. The cascade of sound, movement, and life evaporated in an instant.
The mechanism was flawless: the navigation component stolen from Theo’s designation acted as the perfect mirror.
Through his Full Potential Adaptation, Rex had already experienced the initial shock of the temporal freeze that first contact shudder, where reality stutters before the mind catches up.
But now, the adaptation had fully extended its coverage, stitching his consciousness into the frozen moment.
Two seconds of absolute, terrifying stillness. Then, the adaptation locked in.
Rex began to move. He walked through the silent city like a ghost haunting a museum of corpses.
Pigeons were suspended mid-flight, their wings locked in impossible angles, feathers frozen in the air like shards of glass.
Reconstruction crews were statues of flesh and steel, caught mid-swing, their faces twisted in expressions of mundane labor that now looked grotesque in their immobility.
To Rex, the world had become a silent photograph, and he was the only living thing capable of breaking its frame.
’This is the silence before the scream,’ Rex thought, his boots making no sound on the cobblestones. ’The silence of a god who doesn’t know he’s already been betrayed.’
He reached into the fabric of reality, applying dimensional manipulation directly to the precise dimensional address he had extracted from Theo. He didn’t need a portal; he didn’t need a gateway.

He was constructing something far more dangerous. At the interface where his teleportation skill’s spatial navigation met the dimensional manipulation’s cross-layer traversal, a new capability crystallized: directional movement through dimensional layers without a standard anchor point.
He was slipping between the stitches of existence itself.
Then, he felt it: the layer boundary.
For his entire existence in Erosyne, the physical plane had been his only truth: the texture of air, the weight of gravity, and the solidity of stone.
But the boundary to the adjacent layer wasn’t a wall or a barrier. It was a transition of medium. It felt like stepping from the thinness of air into the crushing, viscous embrace of deep water.
The reality around him rippled, the colors bleeding at the edges as the fundamental laws of physics began to warp.
Rex pushed through.
The world exploded into amber gold.
He emerged not into a place, but into a concept. Kaeleth’s domain was not composed of mountains, sky, or seas.
It was composed of the very temporal symbols. Rex had witnessed during the God’s brief communications with the mortal world the complex, looping notations that mapped time’s properties.
But here, there was no parchment, no sky to hold them. The symbols were the environment.

The ambient medium of this realm was a living, breathing notational framework. Great spirals of golden glyphs writhed through the amber void like celestial serpents; cascading waterfalls of mathematical symbols flowed through the air, each one a heartbeat of time itself.
This was the substrate of eternity manifested as reality. To stand here was to stand inside the clockwork of the universe, where every symbol was a law and every motion was a second passing.
’Magnificent,’ Rex thought, his eyes reflecting the golden chaos. ’A kingdom built of math and memory.’
’How fragile it must be when the equation changes.’
He immediately checked his Presence Manipulationpresence manipulation. The divine class suppression was holding steady at its baseline.

He could feel the domain’s defensive architecture, the ancient, automatic sentinels of Kaeleth’s will brushing against him like invisible fingers. He watched the invisible gauges of his own power as they interacted with the realm’s defenses.
The domain’s consciousness registered him. But it did not register a predator.
It did not register a usurper.

Through the active feedback of his compression, Rex confirmed the deception: Kaeleth’s defenses read him as nothing more than a moderately capable mortal reincarnator, a stray soul who had stumbled through an unusual navigation method.
To the god’s domain, Rex was not a threat to be eliminated; he was a curiosity, a bug caught in the gears that was too small to break the machine.
’A curiosity,’ Rex mused, a cold, predatory smile spreading across his face. ’Let them think that.’
’Let them marvel at the anomaly before I tear their heart out.’
With the confidence of an assassin who has already won, Rex turned away from the border and walked deeper into the golden heart of the domain.
At the heart of the amber gold vortex, Rex found him.
Kaeleth was not the distant, ethereal silhouette that appeared in mortal prayers or divine communications.

Here, in the sanctum of eternity, the God of Time was not a being inhabiting a space; he was the space. He was the convergence of every looping symbol, every cascading glyph, every heartbeat of chronological flow.
Kaeleth was the environment expressing itself with terrible, singular intent, a consciousness woven into the very fabric of the temporal framework.
But even a god was not immune to distraction.
Kaeleth was focused on a visualization bleeding through the domain’s ambient medium. Rex watched as the god observed Aethelgard.
The city’s entire timeline was laid bare in a grotesque, beautiful display of temporal notation. It wasn’t merely an archive; it was a live diagnostic.
Rex could see the jagged scars in the timeline where his own temporal distortion field had torn through the fabric of reality, the anomalous patterns showing the ripple effects of his violence.
He could see the collapse of those fields, the way time had buckled and groaned under his weight, and the countless lives that had been frayed and broken in the process.
And then, Rex saw what held the gods’ attention.
There was a void. A specific, screaming absence in the timeline where Theo’s designation should have been.
A hole in existence where a divine signature had once burned bright, now replaced by a hollow nothingness. Theo was gone, erased, dismantled, and rewritten out of the cosmic ledger.
Kaeleth was staring at that absence. He was studying the wound Rex had left in reality.
Rex did not hesitate. He stepped forward, closing the distance until he stood approximately thirty meters from the God’s central manifestation.
He stopped, his boots planted firmly on a floor of swirling equations.
’Now,’ Rex thought. ’Let’s stop pretending.’
With a deliberate flick of his will, Rex shattered the illusion. He dropped the Presence Manipulation suppression.
It wasn’t a gradual release; it was an explosion. His full divine class signature erupted from his core, flooding the amber medium with the violent force of a supernova breaking through a shell.
The compressed power he had been holding back surged outward, expanding with a hungry, predatory quality that demanded recognition.
The golden symbols around Rex recoiled as if struck by a physical blow, the mathematical notations fracturing and spinning wildly in the wake of his true nature.
Kaeleth’s attention snapped away from the visualization. The God’s consciousness pivoted, tearing itself away from the ghost of Theo to face the reality standing before him.

In that instant, the divine register shifted. For the first time since Rex’s signature had first flickered across Kaeleth’s observation functions, the God’s perception produced a reaction that Rex had been orchestrating since the moment he stepped into Lustia’s domain.
It was a reaction that transcended language, biology, or mortal emotion. It was recognizable across every possible divine expression mechanism.
Fear.
This was not the trembling of a mortal throat or the racing of a human heart. This was something far more profound.

This was the existential terror of an ancient entity, a being that had maintained its absolute dominion for two thousand years, an entity that had developed a perfect, unerring instinct for what constituted a threat to its continued existence.
Kaeleth’s entire being was screaming a single warning: ’This is not a trespasser. This is an end.’

The amber gold symbols that formed Kaeleth’s body began to writhe in panic. They reorganized with terrifying speed, shifting from the fluid motion of ambient presence into the rigid, sharpened configurations of active engagement.
The environment itself began to harden, forming weapons of pure chronological force as the god prepared to defend his throne.
But Rex was already moving.

He didn’t run; he simply ceased to be where he was and existed where he needed to be. He crossed those thirty meters in the infinitesimal span between Rex’s signature release and Kaeleth’s instinctive shift into combat form.
He moved through the space between seconds, faster than thought, faster than the God could react to the threat he now understood.
What Rex produced in that crossing was not a spell. It was not a technique.
It was not a calculated attack.
It was a thought made manifest through absolute violence.

chapters.title: Chapter 1063. You Played With Fire Because You Thought the Room Was Empty
paragraphs: Rex didn’t reach for a weapon. He didn’t summon a blade of divine energy or prepare a spell that would crack the foundations of the domain.
Instead, his hand moved with a casual, almost insulting familiarity toward his left jacket pocket.
He pulled something out.
The throw was not the graceful arc of a telekinetic spell or the calculated trajectory of a seasoned warrior. It was something far more unsettling.
It was a flat, human throw, the dismissive toss of a man throwing a piece of trash across a room. The throw lacked any pretense of respect for its target.

The object sailed through the amber gold haze, cutting through the swirling temporal symbols like a stone through water. It landed with a wet, sickening thud at the very center of Kaeleth’s manifestation.
Kaeleth, the God of Time, whose consciousness spanned millennia, froze. The entire domain seemed to stutter.
The cascading glyphs slowed their rotation, the golden light dimming as the God’s attention locked onto the object that had violated his sanctum.
For one suspended moment, there was only the sound of the universe holding its breath.
Kaeleth looked down at what had arrived. Then, he looked up at Rex.
It was Theo’s head.
But it was not a head in any mortal sense. It was worse.
Through the brutal application of Soul Manipulation’s object creation function, Rex had not merely killed a boy; he had externalized the wound itself.
He had taken the broken part of the Temporal Designation, the raw, spiritual essence that had once linked the boy to the God’s power, and made it into a horrifying, undeniable form.
In the soul register’s spatial representation, the component bore the exact, twisted shape of the soul signature at the moment of investment.

Rex had forced that abstract concept into reality as a physical trophy: a grotesque, gore-slicked skull with eyes that still seemed to hold the fading echo of divine recognition. It was a message written in bone and stolen divinity. It was the physical manifestation of a severed connection.
Rex stood there, his silhouette sharp against the golden chaos. His expression was not one of triumph nor of rage.
It was worse. It was the flat, hollow indifference of a man who had simply completed a tedious chore.
He looked at the God of Time with the same detached attention one might give to a malfunctioning clock.
"You had," Rex said, his voice cutting through the divine silence like a scalpel through silk, "an Apostle for approximately twelve hours."
The words hung in the air, heavier than any spell. They were a mockery of Kaeleth’s eternal nature, a reminder that even divine appointments could be slaughtered and discarded like carrion.
Rex’s eyes remained fixed on Kaeleth’s shifting, panicked form. There was no hesitation in his stance, no tremor in his voice.
He had arrived exactly where he intended to be, and he was not about to perform any grandiosity for the benefit of the audience.
"That is," Rex added, his voice dropping to a cold, venomous whisper that seemed to vibrate through the very symbols of the domain, "a very short tenure."
The moment the words left Rex’s lips, the amber gold reality of the domain didn’t just react; it screamed.
Kaeleth’s form abandoned all pretense of ambient presence. The God of Time fully engaged.
The temporal substrate of the domain, the very foundation of existence in this space, shifted from a flowing river into a crushing tidal wave.

This was not a targeted working, not a spell aimed at a target; this was the domain-level expression of absolute temporal authority. It was the weight of two thousand years of chronological dominion asserting itself as a physical force.
Rex felt the impact.
It wasn’t a blow to his flesh; it was a blow to his continuity. The initial impact of a powerful divine action hit Rex’s body on all levels at once—physical, spiritual, and time-related.
For a microsecond, the God’s will forcibly collapsed and recollapsed Rex’s body, transforming it from a solid object into a series of probability waves.
His bones groaned under the pressure of centuries passing in an instant; his blood felt as though it were attempting to flow backward while simultaneously freezing in his veins.
’This is the pressure of eternity,’ Rex thought through the static of the temporal assault. ’The universe is trying to remind me that I am an intruder.’
Inside his mind, his full potential adaptation roared to life. It didn’t fight the pressure; it consumed it.
It treated the divine onslaught as raw data, a foreign language that needed to be learned, parsed, and internalized.
[Analysis in progress.]
[Temporal Substrate Integration: 12%... 34%... 67%...]
Kaeleth watched. For two millennia, the God had never encountered an entity that could withstand the full expression of his domain without being reduced to scattered atoms or ancient dust.
He watched Rex through those six seconds with a growing, divine confusion, the celestial equivalent of a predator seeing its prey begin to mimic its own claws.
The information Rex was providing was not just unexpected; it was fundamentally incompatible with God’s understanding of reality.
[Analysis Complete.]
Rex felt the temporal substrate reach for him again, attempting to unravel his cellular structure, to twist his timeline into a knot of nonexistence.
But when it touched him, it found nothing to grasp. The adaptation had already mapped the frequency, the texture, and the authority of the domain.
Rex was no longer an intruder; he was becoming a native.
Rex raised his head, his eyes clear and terrifyingly calm amidst the golden storm.
"I have your full domain expression in coverage now," Rex said.
His voice was unnaturally steady, carrying through the howling temporal winds. "Thank you for the complete data set."
Kaeleth’s reaction was visceral. His form convulsed within the ambient medium, a divine spasm of outrage that sent shockwaves through the golden glyphs.
The symbols around them shattered like glass, raining down as sharp fragments of crystallized time that hissed as they dissolved.
Rex didn’t flinch. He began to walk forward.
Each step was a deliberate violation of God’s authority.
"You cheated," Rex said.

The statement was flat, devoid of accusation, delivered with the clinical detachment of a judge reading a verdict. "Not in the mortal sense, there is no rule you have broken, no law you have violated."
"You operated within the margins."
"But in the divine framework? You played with fire because you thought the room was empty."
His boots crunched on the fragments of shattered time. He stopped five meters from the center of Kaeleth’s wrath.
"You played with the one variable you couldn’t control," Rex continued, his voice growing colder. "You provoked an escalation that the divine code was never designed to contain."
Rex’s gaze locked onto the god’s shifting, luminous core. "I am going to be direct with you about what happens next."
"Because you are entitled to the direct version before the end."
Kaeleth remained silent, but the domain itself screamed his fury. Every available ounce of divine power was channeled into his manifestation.
Through Divine Perception, Rex could read the full picture: Kaeleth had committed everything. He had poured every resource, every fragment of his authority, into this moment of confrontation.
He was a god standing at the edge of an abyss, throwing everything he owned into the dark to see if it would stop the fall.
"You contracted with Celestina," Rex said, dismantling the God’s gambit piece by piece. "The contract was a masterpiece of exploitation."

"It was Celestina’s plan for controlling Aethelgard’s reincarnators, your plan for dealing with what your observation function calls timeline disruptions, and the common plan of the agreement, which isn’t technically banned because the divine code’s unclear contract rule was something the creators didn’t see coming."
Rex leaned forward slightly, the golden light casting deep, predatory shadows across his face.
"You thought the ambiguity was your shield."

"You thought you could use the loophole to eliminate a threat like Theo without triggering a cascade." Rex’s lips curled into something that wasn’t quite a smile. "But you forgot one thing about loopholes, Kaeleth."

’This is the pressure of eternity,’ Rex thought through the static of the temporal assault. ’The universe is trying to remind me that I am an intruder.’
Inside his mind, his full potential adaptation roared to life.
It didn’t fight the pressure; it consumed it.
It treated the divine onslaught as raw data, a foreign language that needed to be learned, parsed, and internalized.
[Analysis in progress.]
[Temporal Substrate Integration: 12%...
Kaeleth watched.
For two millennia, the God had never encountered an entity that could withstand the full expression of his domain without being reduced to scattered atoms or ancient dust.
He watched Rex through those six seconds with a growing, divine confusion, the celestial equivalent of a predator seeing its prey begin to mimic its own claws.
The information Rex was providing was not just unexpected; it was fundamentally incompatible with God’s understanding of reality.
[Analysis Complete.]
Rex felt the temporal substrate reach for him again, attempting to unravel his cellular structure, to twist his timeline into a knot of nonexistence.
But when it touched him, it found nothing to grasp.
The adaptation had already mapped the frequency, the texture, and the authority of the domain.
Rex was no longer an intruder; he was becoming a native.
Rex raised his head, his eyes clear and terrifyingly calm amidst the golden storm.
"I have your full domain expression in coverage now," Rex said.
His voice was unnaturally steady, carrying through the howling temporal winds.
"Thank you for the complete data set."
Kaeleth’s reaction was visceral.
His form convulsed within the ambient medium, a divine spasm of outrage that sent shockwaves through the golden glyphs.
The symbols around them shattered like glass, raining down as sharp fragments of crystallized time that hissed as they dissolved.
Rex didn’t flinch.
He began to walk forward.
Each step was a deliberate violation of God’s authority.
"You cheated," Rex said.
The statement was flat, devoid of accusation, delivered with the clinical detachment of a judge reading a verdict.
"Not in the mortal sense, there is no rule you have broken, no law you have violated."
"You operated within the margins."
"But in the divine framework?
You played with fire because you thought the room was empty."
His boots crunched on the fragments of shattered time.
He stopped five meters from the center of Kaeleth’s wrath.
"You played with the one variable you couldn’t control," Rex continued, his voice growing colder.
"You provoked an escalation that the divine code was never designed to contain."
Rex’s gaze locked onto the god’s shifting, luminous core.
"I am going to be direct with you about what happens next."
"Because you are entitled to the direct version before the end."
Kaeleth remained silent, but the domain itself screamed his fury.
Every available ounce of divine power was channeled into his manifestation.
Through Divine Perception, Rex could read the full picture: Kaeleth had committed everything.
He had poured every resource, every fragment of his authority, into this moment of confrontation.
He was a god standing at the edge of an abyss, throwing everything he owned into the dark to see if it would stop the fall.
"You contracted with Celestina," Rex said, dismantling the God’s gambit piece by piece.
"The contract was a masterpiece of exploitation."

"It was Celestina’s plan for controlling Aethelgard’s reincarnators, your plan for dealing with what your observation function calls timeline disruptions, and the common plan of the agreement, which isn’t technically banned because the divine code’s unclear contract rule was something the creators didn’t see coming."
Rex leaned forward slightly, the golden light casting deep, predatory shadows across his face.
"You thought the ambiguity was your shield."
"You thought you could use the loophole to eliminate a threat like Theo without triggering a cascade." Rex’s lips curled into something that wasn’t quite a smile.
"But you forgot one thing about loopholes, Kaeleth."

chapters.title: Chapter 1064. Firing Bullets at a Man Who Had Already Learned How to Become a Bullet
paragraphs: Rex met Kaeleth’s perceptual equivalent of eyes, two blazing vortices of chronological data that burned with the fury of a collapsing star. For a moment, the two stood locked in a silent, terrifying standoff: the ancient architect of eternity versus the anomaly that had learned to speak his language.
"The contract is over," Rex said.
His voice didn’t carry emotion; it carried finality. "The leverage you thought you held has evaporated."
"Celestina’s operational network in the Underlayer has been systematically erased."
"Her surface network is being dismantled as we speak... The time loop architecture you relied upon to cage this reality has collapsed into static."
Rex took another step, the golden floor cracking beneath his weight.
"And you?" Rex’s voice dropped to a predator’s purr. "You are standing in your own sanctum, naked before a mortal who has not only survived your wrath but has learned to breathe your air."
"I have adapted to everything your domain produces."
"Your power is no longer your weapon... it is my fuel."
Rex didn’t raise his hands. He didn’t need to.
He simply reached out with his mind and seized the fundamental concept of weight.
[Gravity Manipulation: Active.]
This was not the blunt force trauma of a meteor strike. This was something far more intimate and excruciating.
Rex applied a targeted force differential, a precision pressure designed not to shatter the surface but to find the exact frequency of the soul register anchor.
Every divine entity requires a metaphysical "hook" to maintain its coherence and authority within its own domain; it is the nail that holds its divinity to its throne.
Rex found that nail. And he began to press down.

"I am not here to play judge, Kaeleth," Rex said as the first sounds of divine distress began to echo through the domain. "The divine framework’s political consequences for your code violation of the tribunal, the sanctions, and the stripping of your authority will be handled by the framework’s governance structure."
"That is bureaucracy. That is not my domain."
A wet, grinding sound reverberated through the amber void.
Kaeleth’s form began to buckle. The golden symbols that composed the God’s body began to warp and bend unnaturally, folding inward like metal under a hydraulic press.
The divine light flickered violently, casting jagged, strobing shadows across Rex’s impassive face.
"What is my domain," Rex continued, his voice cutting through the shriek of protesting reality, "is the specific operational relationship between your agenda and Aethelgard.
Rex’s eyes flared with a cold, murderous light. He didn’t just increase the power; he tightened the grip.
The pressure intensified exponentially.

The sound changed from grinding to something more visceral—the sound of something fundamental breaking. It was the sound of divine bones snapping, not made of calcium, but of crystallized time and solidified will.
Cracks appeared across Kaeleth’s manifestation, bleeding not red blood, but raw, uncontained temporal energy that sizzled like acid where it touched the floor.
The God’s form began to compress, his massive presence forced into a smaller and smaller space, the divine essence screaming as it was crushed against itself.

Rex watched the god’s agony with the detached interest of a scientist observing a reaction. He felt the feedback through his own senses—the way the gravity warred with the temporal substrate—but he remained unmoved.
"That relationship," Rex said, his words punctuated by the wet crunch of Kaeleth’s collapsing divinity, "is going to end."
Rex didn’t just press the pressure; he drove it home. He channeled his full telekinetic force directly into the soul register’s anchor point, the metaphysical carotid artery of a god.
The reaction from the domain was cataclysmic. Because Rex was addressing the structural foundation rather than the operational surface, the domain didn’t just react; it convulsed.

The amber gold reality began to fracture, not like breaking glass, but like tectonic plates grinding together. The divine architecture was being compressed beyond its design parameters, forced into a density that reality itself refused to permit.
The sound was a continuous, low-frequency shriek of reality being crushed.

Kaeleth, sensing his very existence slipping into the void of compression, unleashed a working. A torrent of temporal distortions accelerated entropy and reversed causality, slamming into Rex, attempting to age him into dust and unmake him into nothingness simultaneously.
[Adaptation engaged.]
Rex’s body twisted, his muscles corded like steel cables as his cellular structure reorganized mid-assault. He absorbed the entropy, neutralized the reversal, and stood unmoved.
Kaeleth roared a sound that was less a voice and more the grinding of centuries and produced a second working.
This one was a spatial severance, a series of temporal blades designed to cut through the concept of ’distance’ to slice Rex apart from within.
[Adaptation engaged.]
Rex’s nervous system flickered as he remapped his own spatial coordinates, dancing through the blades of time as if they were mere shadows.

Desperate, Kaeleth reached deeper than he ever had before. He summoned a third working, the domain’s native expression, which was the most sophisticated and devastating mechanism available to a God of Time.

It was a complete collapse of the local timeline, a singularity of ’Now’ that intended to freeze Rex in a moment of eternal, excruciating stasis while his body was torn apart by the sheer force of time trying to exist in two places at once.
Rex met the singularity head-on. His vision blurred as the first contact effect tore through his consciousness.
For four point two seconds, Rex existed in a state of pure agony as his organs felt themselves being pulled across millennia.
His bones creaked and splintered under the temporal shear, blood spraying from his nose and mouth as his capillaries burst under the strain of existing outside of linear time.
’Faster,’ Rex thought through the white noise of pain. ’I need to be faster than time itself.’
[First Contact Effect: Absorbed.]
[Temporal Singularity: Analyzed.]
[Adaptation: Complete.]
Rex spat a glob of crimson blood onto the golden floor, his eyes burning with a terrifying, inhuman clarity. The pain was gone, replaced by a cold, predatory certainty.
He had learned God’s final language.
"Last category," Rex said, his voice dripping with the satisfaction of a predator who has cornered a wounded animal. "Same as Theo."
He began to close the remaining distance. Each step was a death knell.
What followed in Kaeleth’s domain was not the prolonged, desperate struggle Rex had endured in the streets with Theo. That had been a trial by fire; this was an execution.
The Full Potential Adaptation had been building its library during every second of the previous confrontation.

Every temporal blade, every entropic wave, and every spatial distortion—Rex had cataloged them all. His coverage list was no longer a collection of defenses; it was a complete map of Kaeleth’s entire arsenal.
Kaeleth’s divine eyes widened. For the first time in two thousand years, the God felt something he had forgotten existed: helplessness.
He threw everything he had left, every last shred of his authority, and every hidden mechanism of his domain at Rex.
He unleashed chronal storms, causality loops, and reality-warping distortions that would have obliterated entire civilizations.
But Rex walked through them as if walking through a light rain.

Every attack hit Rex’s adaptive field, and he died. Every divine mechanism was met with the perfect counter frequency. The God of Time was firing bullets at a man who had already learned how to become a bullet.
Kaeleth had run out of new mechanisms. He was standing naked before a mortal who held the blueprint to his entire existence.
Everything he was, everything he could do, was already in Rex’s coverage.
