The domain’s floor beneath Rex’s boots, the very air molecules filling his lungs, and the jagged shards of reality still drifting from the earlier fracture—all of it was seized and dragged into a localized temporal compression.
This wasn’t the acceleration field from before.
This wasn’t about speed; it was about exhaustion.
It aged the specific patch of reality.
Rex stood in through several subjective centuries in the heartbeat it took Kaeleth to close his fist.
Rex’s Adaptation screamed in confusion.
It had no prior mechanism to draw from.
How do you adapt to the universe simply deciding you have already lived your entire life?
Rex felt his skin do something skin was never meant to do.

A papery, ancient brittleness seized his flesh, then receded in the same half second the nauseating sensation of a body being shown the full, horrific spectrum of its own death by age, only to be yanked back from the brink before the preview finished.
His Infinite Regeneration fired reflexively, a desperate, panicked response that began patching cellular damage that hadn’t even fully manifested yet.
It was a biological paradox: his body was healing wounds that were still in the process of being imagined by time.
’Fuck...’ Rex’s mind clawed through the vertigo. ’My body doesn’t know what to fight.’
’It’s fighting itself.’
He didn’t have time to process the wrongness.
He couldn’t afford to think; he could only act.
"You want to age me?" Rex roared through gritted teeth, blood spattering from his gums as his own jawbone creaked under the temporal strain.
"Then age the ground beneath me first!"
With a guttural scream of exertion, Rex unleashed his telekinesis at full, uncontrolled output.
He didn’t aim at Kaeleth; he aimed at the medium.
He drove his force straight down through the compressed patch of floor beneath his own feet, forcing his power into the structural level of the domain’s reality.
He sought to punch through the very fabric of the accelerated moment.
The result was catastrophic.

The localized compression sheared away from the rest of the domain’s temporal fabric with a sound that wasn’t a sound; it was a wet, tearing silence, the sound of something being violently ripped from the network of existence.
The reality beneath Rex gave way, collapsing into a void of fractured causality.
Rex fell.
He plunged through the hole he had violently carved into the universe.
But Kaeleth was not content to let his prey escape into the depths.
The God followed, his divine robes dissolving, reforming into something far more lethal: a blade of pure, razor-sharp amber gold notation.
Kaeleth was fast, not human fast, not even superpowered fast, but divine fast.
He operated outside the relationship between force and momentum; he simply arrived at his destination slightly before the moment he decided to move.
The amber blade descended like a guillotine of light.
It caught Rex across the ribs.
It didn’t just cut flesh; it cut duration.
Rex felt three seconds of his own existence being torn out of his body like pages ripped from a book mid-sentence.
The wound wasn’t just a gash; it was a hole in his timeline.

The removal produced a lurch of soul-crushing vertigo that had nothing to do with balance and everything to do with the primal horror of a mind suddenly realizing it was missing pieces of its own reality.
Rex slammed onto his back on the reformed floor below the hole, the impact sending a shockwave through his spine that made his vision go white.
Blood hot and crimson, ordinary human blood gushed from his side, pooling beneath him.
His ribs felt like broken glass grinding against his lungs with every ragged breath.
"Is this the limit of your adaptation, Rex?" Kaeleth’s voice descended like a death knell as the god landed gracefully, the amber blade already elongating for the killing stroke.
"To die in fragments?"
Rex stared up at the approaching deity, blood frothing at the corners of his mouth.
His ribs screamed, his side burned with a wound that defied healing, and his mind reeled from the temporal amputation.
But as Kaeleth swung the blade down for the second strike, something shifted in Rex’s eyes.
The panic died.
The pain became nothing more than data.
He didn’t try to block it.
He didn’t raise a shield.
As the blade of pure causality descended toward his throat, Rex’s hand shot upward with the speed of a striking viper.
He grabbed it.

chapters.title: Chapter 1072. Missing Eight Seconds of His Own Life
paragraphs: The Earthen Authority’s grip slammed shut around the amber gold notation. The contact wasn’t just physical; it was a metaphysical violation.
The divine authority burned through Rex’s palm like molten phosphorus, searing through muscle and nerve, eating away at flesh that was already struggling to maintain its own continuity.
But Rex didn’t flinch. His fingers locked around the blade with a strength that defied his broken ribs and hemorrhaging side.
He wasn’t trying to stop the weapon; he was using it as an anchor, a tether to chain the god to his own reality.

With a primal roar that tore at his vocal cords, Rex channeled every remaining ounce of his telekinetic reserves into a single, concentrated point. He drove the force upward, a piston-like strike aimed directly at Kaeleth’s sternum at point-blank range.
’Now. Break him.’
The impact was seismic. Kaeleth’s composure, the millennia of practiced, divine detachment, cracked audibly.

The god recoiled as if struck by a physical sledgehammer, his eyes widening in genuine, unfiltered shock. The amber blade dissolved back into flowing robes as Kaeleth stumbled backward, and the entire domain lurched with him.
The very architecture of reality shuddered and groaned, the way a living body convulses when its heart skips a beat.
"You... you are supposed to be dying," Kaeleth hissed.

His voice had stripped away the careful, administrative calm. What remained was something ancient, something feral, the voice of a predator who had ruled unchallenged for two thousand years and had suddenly discovered how terrifying it was to feel pain.
Rex slumped forward slightly, blood streaming from the gash in his ribs, painting his tan skin in wet crimson. He spat a glob of gore onto the reforming floor and watched it splatter.
A slow, vicious smile spread across his face.
"I noticed," Rex rasped, the words bubbling through the blood in his throat. "But I’m not done playing yet."
The smile was the breaking point. Kaeleth’s face twisted into something monstrous, and he answered with three simultaneous workings.

This was the moment that would later be remembered as the catalyst for Rex’s most violent evolution. It wasn’t just that Kaeleth was holding nothing back; it was that he had stopped believing in strategy.

He had moved past the concept of a ’duel’ and into the territory of ’annihilation.’ He was attacking in an overlapping cascade, a desperate belief that if he could apply enough simultaneous pressure, he could crush the anomaly before it could think.
First came the Temporal Compressiontemporal compression. It was smaller this time, surgical and cruel.

It targeted Rex’s hands specifically, aiming to age his grip into brittle, ancient bone before he could tighten it again. Rex felt his fingers begin to wither, the skin wrinkling into parchment even as his muscles screamed.
Second came the Temporal Severancetemporal severance. Three blade-shaped absences tore through the air like spears of nothingness.
They weren’t physical projectiles; they were wounds in time itself, designed to slice through Rex’s duration from a distance, severing his limbs from the present moment.
Third, and this was the true horror, was the Foundation Collapse. In a fit of divine desperation, Kaeleth didn’t aim at Rex at all.
He aimed at the domain. He began to unravel the very framework of the space they stood in, initiating a scorched earth protocol that would collapse the entire reality around them.
He would rather unmake existence itself than allow Rex to stand victorious within it.
’Three threats.’
’Three simultaneous vectors of annihilation.’
Rex’s Divine Perception flared to life, reading all three workings in the same terrifying instant. His mind screamed.
For the first time since the fight began, his adaptation couldn’t process sequentially. The analysis windows couldn’t wait for one to finish before starting the next.
His brain was forced into parallel processing a brutal, overclocked calculation that sent a spike of agony behind his eyes so intense he thought his skull would split open.
’Think, damn you!’
’Adapt or die!’ his inner voice roared through the static of pain. ’I can’t stop all three!’
’If I try to defend everything, I’ll have nothing left to counter the collapse!!!’
His vision blurred. His brain felt like it was being cooked in his own skull as the parallel processing pushed his consciousness to the breaking point.
He saw the withered skin of his hands, he saw the approaching spears of nonexistence, and he felt the ground beneath him beginning to dissolve into the void.
He had a fraction of a second. A choice between survival and total annihilation.
Rex’s jaw set. His eyes burned with a cold, suicidal clarity.
He made his choice. He let the first two hit him.
The first strike hit with the cruelty of a thousand autumns. The temporal compression seized Rex’s hands, aging the flesh, bone, and sinew into something brittle, ancient, and useless.
For one agonizing heartbeat, his fingers became desiccated husks, the bones cracking like dry twigs under the mere pressure of his own grip. But then, the Infinite Regeneration screamed into action.
It was a desperate, violent gambit, a biological counterattack. The cellular damage was reversed in a nauseating flash of heat, forcing the withered flesh back into its prime.
It was a gamble that cost him precious seconds of focus, but it kept his hands from crumbling into dust.
Then came the Temporal Severance.
The blade-shaped absence tore through his torso like a ghost knife made of pure nothingness. This wasn’t a three-second nick; this was a five-second amputation of his existence.
Rex felt the world vanish. There was no pain in that moment, only an absolute, terrifying void where his consciousness should have been.

When his mind finally reconnected to the timeline, the reconnection felt like being slammed into a concrete wall at full speed. A cold, primal terror flooded his system—a genuine, bone-deep recognition that he was running out of time.

If he took one more hit like that, the slice would be too wide. Whatever reassembled itself on the other side of that void wouldn’t be Rex anymore; it would be something broken, hollowed out, and unrecognizable.
’Not yet,’ Rex snarled internally, his mind racing through the static of agony. ’I can’t let him erase me...’
’Not like this...’
He had spent everything the first two hits had cost him—every ounce of mental focus, every drop of regenerative energy—to stop the third.
As the domain began to unravel, as the foundational framework of Kaeleth’s reality started to collapse inward like a dying star, Rex didn’t try to fix it. He couldn’t reinforce a god’s architecture.
Instead, he did something far more desperate: he braced it.
He plunged his telekinetic will into the fracturing structure of the domain itself. He didn’t act as a builder; he acted as a wedge.

He threw his raw, kinetic stubbornness against the collapsing reality, jamming his power into the cracks like steel struts in a collapsing mine shaft. He was trying to hold a universe together through sheer, brute-force refusal.
The domain screamed.

It wasn’t a sound heard with ears, but a psychic shriek that vibrated through every atom of Rex’s being, the ambient equivalent of a god’s own sanctum crying out as it was asked to survive its own creator’s attempt to murder it.
The space groaned, twisted, and buckled under the strain, but through Rex’s impossible defiance, it held.
Silence fell, heavy and suffocating.
Kaeleth stood amidst the wreckage of his own scorched earth working.

The god’s divine composure was gone, replaced by the ragged breathing of an entity that had just spent resources it hadn’t budgeted for power that should have been eternal, now depleted by the sheer effort of trying to erase a single mortal.
His eyes fixed on Rex, and the horror in them was unmistakable.

Rex was a wreck. He was drenched in blood, his side was a gaping wound that refused to fully close, his hands were still faintly translucent as his cells struggled to reassert their proper age, and he was missing eight seconds of his own life.
He looked like something that should have been dead ten minutes ago.
Yet, he was still standing.
"What... what are you?" Kaeleth demanded.
The words weren’t a question; they were a confession of failure. It was the sound of a two thousand-year-old deity realizing that his entire understanding of the universe had just been proven wrong.
He had no framework, no category, no divine law to explain why this anomaly refused to die.
Rex rolled his shoulders, the movement drawing a wet, sickening pop as something in his back dislocated during the earlier melee slammed back into place.
The regeneration was finally catching up, flooding his system with a painful, overwhelming surge of healing that felt like molten metal running through his veins.
Rex spat a mouthful of blood onto the cracked floor, his eyes locking onto Kaeleth’s with a predator’s intensity.
"I told you already," Rex rasped, his voice gravelly and dangerous. "I’m the thing that happens when nobody’s paying attention to the domain that supposedly doesn’t produce combat capability."

chapters.title: Chapter 1073. A Puzzle to Be Solved, Not a Catastrophe to Be Survived
paragraphs: Rex didn’t wait for the god to process the threat. He moved before the last syllable had even left his lips. His Lustful Villain register triggered a cold, predatory shift in his consciousness that collapsed the distance between intent and execution to absolute zero.
He wasn’t running; he was a blur of violence, a streak of crimson and tan cutting through the divine haze at a speed that Kaeleth’s depleted temporal reserves could no longer track.
The god’s eyes widened, pupils contracting as he realized his reaction time was now measured in seconds while Rex was operating in milliseconds.
What followed was not a fourth exchange. This was not a tactical back-and-forth exchange.
It was an execution wearing the mask of a fight.
Kaeleth had made the fatal error of every immortal who had never tasted defeat: he had treated Rex like a puzzle to be solved rather than a catastrophe to be survived.

He had spent the whole fight trying out different divine powers to see which one could finally defeat Rex, ignoring the clear warning from the first sign of trouble: that none of his powers could control something that didn’t follow the usual rules of cause and effect.
Rex’s fingers slammed shut around Kaeleth’s throat.
The contact was brutal. Rex’s knuckles scraped against the divine flesh, the pressure so immense that the god’s neck tendons strained like steel cables.
Rex wasn’t trying to choke him; he knew divine anatomy didn’t require oxygen. He was anchoring himself. He needed that point of contact.
He needed to bridge the gap between his own corrupted reality and the god’s perfect one so that when he unleashed what came next, there would be no distance for the divine authority to deflect it.

Up close, the illusion of Kaeleth’s divinity shattered completely. Rex’s Divine Perception pierced through the golden radiance and the regal robes, reading the truth that the god’s face couldn’t hide.
Kaeleth was terrified.
Rex could see it in the minute tremors of the god’s eyelids, in the way his divine aura flickered like a dying candle, and in the hollow, desperate emptiness behind those ancient eyes.
The ruler of two millennia was suddenly reduced to something small, something fragile, something mortal.
Rex leaned in, his breath hot against the god’s ear, his voice dropping to a whisper that carried more menace than any roar. The performance was over.
The bravado, the taunts, and the theatricality—all of it fell away, leaving only the raw, unfiltered hunger of the predator.
"This," Rex said, the words dripping with a cold, inevitable finality, "is the part where you find out what happens after."
The domain itself seemed to recoil. The very fabric of space held its breath, the specific, suffocating silence of a reality that knows its owner is about to lose control.
The architecture groaned, the light dimmed to a sickly amber, and for one suspended moment, time itself seemed to freeze in anticipation of the slaughter.
Then, the fourteen minutes ended.
The slaughter began not with a bang, but with the terrifying precision of a god realizing he was being hunted by something that learned faster than he could kill.
Kaeleth’s desperation manifested first as a Temporal Slowtemporal slowdown. He threw his will against the fabric of reality, attempting to drag Rex’s personal timeline into thick, viscous molasses.
For a heartbeat, Rex felt the universe turn to honey, every movement requiring an impossible expenditure of effort. But Rex’s adaptation was already screaming.

The system analyzed the god tier implementation the way Kaeleth manipulated the fundamental constant of speed, and within five point eight agonizing seconds, Rex’s consciousness had mapped the divine architecture of the ability.
He didn’t just resist it; he learned how to exist within it.
"Is that it?" Rex’s inner voice growled through the mental static. "Is that all the power of two millennia gets you?"
Kaeleth’s face contorted with fury. He reached deeper, pulling at the seams of causality itself.
He unleashed a timeline fracture.
This was something Rex had never encountered. Theo’s mortal-level abilities hadn’t touched this level of atrocity.
As the fracture struck, Rex’s sense of self didn’t just slow; it shattered. His consciousness splintered into a thousand jagged shards.
One version of Rex was screaming; another was already dead; a third was still standing frozen. His very existence became incoherent, a kaleidoscopic nightmare of simultaneous, conflicting presents.
It felt like his brain was being fed through a meat grinder of pure information.
’Four point nine seconds.’
Four point nine seconds of absolute, existential horror. Then, with a psychic wrench that felt like tearing his own soul back together, Rex snapped back into coherence.
The adaptation had done its work. It had tasted the incoherence and learned how to stitch itself back together.
The coverage was extended: Timeline Fractures acquired.
Rex didn’t pause to recover. He channeled his fury through his Telekinesistelekinesis, not as a blunt instrument, but as a scalpel of pure rage.
He slammed the force against Kaeleth’s position with the specific, directed violence of someone who had just survived being unmade.
The impact was devastating. Kaeleth was hurled backward eight meters, his divine robes fluttering like wounded wings as he skidded across the sanctum floor.
"You monster," Kaeleth hissed, blood golden and luminous seeping from the corner of his mouth. "You are not a man...!"
"You are a cancer on reality!
"Then consider yourself infected," Rex spat.
Kaeleth rose, his eyes blazing with a cold, apocalyptic light. He didn’t try to slow or fracture this time.
He went for the kill. He deployed the Temporal Freeze.
Unlike Theo’s area of effect stop, this was a surgical strike. Kaeleth targeted Rex’s personal timeline with god-tier precision, attempting to halt Rex’s existence entirely.
For three point one seconds, Rex ceased to be. He didn’t just stop moving; he stopped happening.
He became a statue in the middle of a rushing river, a fixed point of nothingness in a moving world.
’Three point one seconds.’

The adaptation seized the pattern before the freeze could become permanent. Rex’s consciousness reconnected with a jarring, nauseating lurch, the sensation of a mind being forcibly yanked back into a body that had forgotten how to breathe.
His lungs burned, his heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped animal, and his vision strobed with residual temporal afterimages.
But Rex was already moving. He was done playing with time.
He reached down with the Earthen Authority, seizing the very bones of the domain. The stone-analogous substance beneath his feet groaned and shrieked as he tore it apart.
With terrifying precision, he fused the debris into a massive, jagged geological construct—a projectile of compressed mineral density designed to shatter anything in its path.
This wasn’t a temporal attack. It wasn’t a concept or a law.
It was pure, unadulterated physical force. And in the calculus of combat, physical force possessed a unique advantage: it operated on a different dimensional plane than temporal defenses.
You could slow time, but you couldn’t slow the momentum of a mountain once it was already moving.
Rex launched it. The projectile tore through the air with a sound like a collapsing building, a screaming comet of stone and fury aimed directly at Kaeleth’s chest.
Kaeleth’s eyes narrowed. With a flick of his wrist, he raised a barrier of compressed light, deflecting the projectile.
The impact sent sparks of divine energy cascading across the chamber like fireworks, but the god remained unbowed.

Kaeleth’s desperation manifested first as a Temporal Slowtemporal slowdown.
He threw his will against the fabric of reality, attempting to drag Rex’s personal timeline into thick, viscous molasses.
For a heartbeat, Rex felt the universe turn to honey, every movement requiring an impossible expenditure of effort.
But Rex’s adaptation was already screaming.

The system analyzed the god tier implementation the way Kaeleth manipulated the fundamental constant of speed, and within five point eight agonizing seconds, Rex’s consciousness had mapped the divine architecture of the ability.
He didn’t just resist it; he learned how to exist within it.
"Is that it?" Rex’s inner voice growled through the mental static.
"Is that all the power of two millennia gets you?"
Kaeleth’s face contorted with fury.
He reached deeper, pulling at the seams of causality itself.
He unleashed a timeline fracture.
This was something Rex had never encountered.
Theo’s mortal-level abilities hadn’t touched this level of atrocity.
As the fracture struck, Rex’s sense of self didn’t just slow; it shattered.
His consciousness splintered into a thousand jagged shards.
One version of Rex was screaming; another was already dead; a third was still standing frozen.
His very existence became incoherent, a kaleidoscopic nightmare of simultaneous, conflicting presents.
It felt like his brain was being fed through a meat grinder of pure information.
’Four point nine seconds.’
Four point nine seconds of absolute, existential horror.
Then, with a psychic wrench that felt like tearing his own soul back together, Rex snapped back into coherence.
The adaptation had done its work.
It had tasted the incoherence and learned how to stitch itself back together.
The coverage was extended: Timeline Fractures acquired.
Rex didn’t pause to recover.
He channeled his fury through his Telekinesistelekinesis, not as a blunt instrument, but as a scalpel of pure rage.
He slammed the force against Kaeleth’s position with the specific, directed violence of someone who had just survived being unmade.
The impact was devastating.
Kaeleth was hurled backward eight meters, his divine robes fluttering like wounded wings as he skidded across the sanctum floor.
"You monster," Kaeleth hissed, blood golden and luminous seeping from the corner of his mouth.
"You are not a man...!"
"You are a cancer on reality!
"Then consider yourself infected," Rex spat.
Kaeleth rose, his eyes blazing with a cold, apocalyptic light.
He didn’t try to slow or fracture this time.
He went for the kill.
He deployed the Temporal Freeze.
Unlike Theo’s area of effect stop, this was a surgical strike.
Kaeleth targeted Rex’s personal timeline with god-tier precision, attempting to halt Rex’s existence entirely.
For three point one seconds, Rex ceased to be.
He didn’t just stop moving; he stopped happening.
He became a statue in the middle of a rushing river, a fixed point of nothingness in a moving world.
’Three point one seconds.’
The adaptation seized the pattern before the freeze could become permanent.
Rex’s consciousness reconnected with a jarring, nauseating lurch, the sensation of a mind being forcibly yanked back into a body that had forgotten how to breathe.
His lungs burned, his heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped animal, and his vision strobed with residual temporal afterimages.
But Rex was already moving.
He was done playing with time.
He reached down with the Earthen Authority, seizing the very bones of the domain.
The stone-analogous substance beneath his feet groaned and shrieked as he tore it apart.
With terrifying precision, he fused the debris into a massive, jagged geological construct—a projectile of compressed mineral density designed to shatter anything in its path.
This wasn’t a temporal attack.
It wasn’t a concept or a law.
It was pure, unadulterated physical force.
And in the calculus of combat, physical force possessed a unique advantage: it operated on a different dimensional plane than temporal defenses.
You could slow time, but you couldn’t slow the momentum of a mountain once it was already moving.
Rex launched it.
The projectile tore through the air with a sound like a collapsing building, a screaming comet of stone and fury aimed directly at Kaeleth’s chest.
Kaeleth’s eyes narrowed.
With a flick of his wrist, he raised a barrier of compressed light, deflecting the projectile.
The impact sent sparks of divine energy cascading across the chamber like fireworks, but the god remained unbowed.

chapters.title: Chapter 1074. A Mathematician Facing a Broken Equation
paragraphs: Rex didn’t flinch when the stone comet shattered against Kaeleth’s barrier. In fact, he had counted every microsecond of the deflection.

His Divine Perception wasn’t just watching the attack; it was dissecting the barrier’s response. He felt the way the divine light rippled, the specific harmonic frequency at which Kaeleth’s defensive architecture stabilized itself.
He now knew exactly where the god’s physical invulnerability ended and his temporal authority began.
’He’s relying too much on the rules of time,’ Rex thought, a dark, hungry smile spreading across his blood-slicked lips. ’But he forgot about the rules of weight.’
"Let’s see how you deflect something that doesn’t care about time," Rex growled.
He unleashed Gravity Manipulation.

This wasn’t a magical spell or a system-based energy pulse; it was a fundamental manipulation of the physical medium. In his previous engagement in the Underlayer, Rex had confirmed that gravity was a blunt instrument that bypassed the elegant defenses of temporal manipulators.
Kaeleth could slow a spell, he could fracture a timeline, but he couldn’t stop the very fabric of space from wanting to collapse inward.
Kaeleth’s eyes widened. For the first time, the god’s composure didn’t just slip; it evaporated.
He felt the sudden, impossible wrongness of his own domain. The air grew thick, not with magic, but with sheer, crushing mass.
The stone floor beneath him didn’t just crack; it imploded, the atoms themselves screaming as they were forced toward a single, crushing epicenter: Kaeleth’s own body.
"What... what is this?" Kaeleth gasped, his voice strained as the divine pressure began to pin his limbs to his sides. "This isn’t temporal magic! This is—"
"This is physics, you arrogant bastard," Rex interrupted.
The compression wasn’t enough to crush Kaeleth’s divine form; his body was too ancient, too structurally reinforced by millennia of power, but it was constraining.
It turned the god’s own sanctum into a vice, trapping him in a localized well of immense pressure that made every movement an agonizing struggle against tons of invisible force.
Rex seized the opening. He moved like liquid shadow through the crushing field, his Martial Arts Mastery activating with lethal efficiency.
He wasn’t just fighting a god; he was fighting a target that was being forced into a predictable, compressed position.
Rex became a whirlwind of bone-breaking violence.
Crack.
The first strike, a palm heel to the sternum, didn’t just hit; it transmitted a shockwave designed to bypass divine armor, rattling Kaeleth’s very essence.
Thud.
The second strike, a brutal elbow to the ribs, sent a cascade of golden ichor spraying from the god’s side as the divine structure buckled.
Snap.
The third strike, a spinning kick to the temple, was timed to the exact millisecond Kaeleth tried to reassert his temporal control, disrupting his focus.
Then came the fourth hit.
Rex channeled everything. He didn’t just use strength; he used the Gravity Manipulation itself, carrying the crushing force of the gravitational well through his fist.
He calibrated the frequency of the strike to match the resonant frequency of Kaeleth’s own domain structure, the very ’song’ that kept the god’s power coherent.
The punch landed with the sound of a world breaking.
It wasn’t a tactical grunt of pain. It wasn’t a calculated roar of defiance.
Kaeleth screamed.
It was a raw, primal, involuntary shriek of pure agony. It was the sound of something eternal being violated by something mortal.

The strike didn’t just hurt; it shattered his divine coherence. For a moment, the god’s very identity flickered, his form destabilizing as the gravitational frequency tore through his spiritual foundation.
The golden light that defined him turned sickly and mottled, bleeding out of him in ragged spurts.

The domain itself reacted to its master’s torment. The sky above the sanctum convulsed, the stars streaking and distorting as the fundamental laws of the space began to unravel in sympathy with Kaeleth’s pain.
The domain shook with the fury of a dying god.

The tremor wasn’t metaphorical. It was a physical violation of reality. When Rex’s fist connected with Kaeleth’s divine coherence, the shockwave didn’t just ripple through the air; it tore through the very medium of space itself.

The amber gold symbols etched into the sanctum’s walls shrieked as they vibrated at a frequency that threatened to liquify stone. Fragments of previous spells and shards of frozen time and petrified earth were caught in the blast, spinning outward like shrapnel in a detonation.
Rex didn’t get swept away. Gritting his teeth, he slammed his power into the Earthen Authority, anchoring his boots into the floor as if he were part of the mountain itself.
His muscles coiled, veins standing out like corded steel beneath his tan skin, as he braced against the feedback.
The shockwave roared past him, a wall of displaced existence that left his ears ringing and his vision swimming with afterimages.
Silence fell.
A heavy, suffocating silence that tasted of copper and burnt divinity.
Kaeleth’s form flickered like a dying hologram before stabilizing. But he was changed.

The regal, overwhelming radiance that had defined his presence at the start of the fight had dimmed. The amber gold symbols swirling around the domain were moving slower now; their rhythmic pulse labored and became arrhythmic.
Through Divine Perception, Rex saw the truth in raw numbers: Kaeleth’s available expression was plummeting. He was bleeding energy, not blood, but the very essence of his authority.
The god stood there, swaying slightly, blood golden, luminous, and thick as syrup dripping from his split lips onto the cracked marble floor.
He looked at Rex, not with the rage of a warrior, but with the cold, terrifying intensity of a mathematician facing a broken equation.
He was calculating.
Rex watched him, his own breathing controlled despite the adrenaline hammering in his chest.
’Look at you,’ Rex thought bitterly. ’Two thousand years of absolute certainty, and now you’re reduced to guessing.’
"The Forbidden God designation," Kaeleth said finally.
His voice was hoarse, stripped of its melodic divinity, carrying only the weight of centuries. "Its amplification effect on your combat parameters... it’s not a static buff."
Rex didn’t move. "Keep talking."

"You entered this domain at the suppressed baseline of Presence Manipulationpresence manipulation," Kaeleth continued, his eyes tracking Rex’s every micro movement with desperate focus. "Then, after the opening exchange, you deployed the Lustful Villain form’s amplification."
"You’re not just stronger, Rex Rexilion... You’re evolving in real time."
"Yes," Rex answered simply, the word a taunt.

"The amplification is proportional to the accumulated desire bonds," Kaeleth muttered, more to himself than to Rex. "Every soul you’ve touched, every conquest in Aethelgard... they are feeding the furnace."
"The current level of your power is exponentially higher than the designation’s initial grant."
"Yes."
"And the Adaptation," Kaeleth’s voice rose with a frantic edge. "The analysis windows are shrinking."
"The time it takes for you to parse my abilities is dropping every second..."
"I’m not fighting a man who learns; I’m fighting a system that consumes my own power to accelerate its own comprehension."
Rex’s gaze hardened. "You’re trying to solve me."

"I am trying to understand the mathematics of your existence," Kaeleth corrected, his hands trembling slightly as he began to weave a new pattern in the air. "Every equation has a solution... Every anomaly has a limit."
"You’re looking for an angle," Rex said, stepping forward, each footfall echoing like a death knell in the emptying sanctum. "A weakness in the math."
"There is always an angle," Kaeleth snapped.
His voice regained a flash of that ancient, unshakable confidence—the arrogance of a being who had never known an unsolvable problem. "There is always a variable I can control."
Rex stopped ten feet from him. The air between them hummed with lethal tension, the smell of blood and burnt ozone thick enough to choke on.
"There’s your mistake," Rex said, his voice dropping to a predator’s growl. "There is an angle for every problem but only for the person who has the capability to implement it."
Rex’s eyes glowed with a cruel, knowing light. "The angle you’re hunting requires you to be faster than my Adaptation’s analysis speed."
"But the problem is, Kaeleth... the more you fight, the faster I get."
"Every time you strike, every time you try to adapt, you’re giving me the real-time data I need to close the loop."
"You’re not solving the equation."
Rex’s lips curled into a savage grin as he prepared to close the distance for the kill.
"You’re writing the answer for me."

chapters.title: Chapter 1075. Working Classes Are Properties of the Domain, Not Inventions
paragraphs: Rex stared through Kaeleth, his eyes not seeing a god but seeing a data stream, a sequence of failures unfolding in real time.

The tension in the sanctum was so thick it felt like breathing liquid mercury. Every ragged breath Kaeleth drew sounded like gravel grinding in a wound, a wet, choking noise that punctuated the terrible silence.
"You made me faster every time you hit me," Rex said, his voice disturbingly calm, almost conversational. "That’s the beauty of it, isn’t it?"
"The Adaptation’s analysis speed isn’t just a passive shield; it’s a learning function."
"It’s a predator that grows stronger with every wound it receives..."
"You weren’t fighting me, Kaeleth... You were training me."
Kaeleth remained silent. His golden blood continued to drip from his chin, spattering against the floor with a rhythmic tap... tap... tap that sounded like a countdown.
His divine composure was gone, replaced by the hollow stare of a man who had just realized he was trapped in a cage of his own making.
"How many times did you hit me?" Rex asked.
He tilted his head, studying the god with clinical detachment.
Kaeleth said nothing. His lips merely trembled, blood frothing at the corners of his mouth.
"Seventeen," Rex stated, each syllable landing like a hammer blow. "I received seventeen distinct first contact mechanisms over the course of this engagement."
"Seventeen separate analysis windows where I had to parse your reality."
"Seventeen coverage extensions where I had to remap my own existence to survive you."
Rex took a step forward. The floor beneath his boot groaned as if protesting his approach.

"And at the end of that seventeenth strike, that last pathetic attempt to fracture my soul, the Adaptation’s analysis speed for temporal class workings was running at approximately forty percent of the initial baseline."
"I’m not learning in increments anymore, Kaeleth..."
"I’m learning in leaps... I’m learning faster than you can think."
Rex began walking toward him. It wasn’t a charge; it was a slow, inexorable march.’
The kind of walk a butcher takes toward a stunned animal.
"You ran out of new things, didn’t you?" Rex’s voice grew darker, more predatory. "The temporal domain’s working set is finite."
"You have a god’s arsenal... you have countless expressions of temporal authority."
"You can slow time, you can loop it, you can fracture it into shards. But they are all just different faces on the same coin."
"They all share one fundamental mechanism."
Rex was ten meters away now. He could see the way Kaeleth’s divine armor was hairline fractured, the way the golden light flickered like a dying candle in a hurricane.

"Once the Adaptation has covered that fundamental mechanism through enough implementations, the coverage extends to the general case," Rex explained, his inner monologue a cold stream of tactical certainty. ’He’s cornered.’
He’s a king with no kingdom left, a scholar with no words left.’
’Now, I break what’s left.’
"It doesn’t matter which flavor of time you throw at me... I’ve already learned the recipe."
The distance closed.
Nine meters.
Eight.

"You cannot produce a new mechanism," Rex said, his voice dropping to a guttural whisper that seemed to vibrate in Kaeleth’s very bones. "You’ve been practicing the same divine arts for two thousand years."
"You’re a master of your domain, yes. But mastery isn’t invention."
"You cannot invent a new class of working on demand, because working classes aren’t things you do."
"They are properties of the domain itself. And your domain? Your domain is exhausted."
Rex stopped five meters away. He stood there, a mountain of scarred muscle and murderous intent, looming over the broken deity.
The air between them crackled with the static of Rex’s unleashed power, a physical pressure that made the very air scream.
Rex’s eyes locked onto Kaeleth’s, no mercy, no hesitation, only the cold satisfaction of a predator who has already won.
"You’re out of options," Rex said.
Kaeleth raised his gaze.

There was something profoundly wrong with the way he looked at Rex. When a mortal runs out of options, they collapse into a predictable biological cascade: sweat, dilated pupils, the frantic heaving of lungs, and the primal stench of terror.
But a god? A god’s desperation was something far more alien.
Kaeleth’s defeat didn’t manifest as fear; it manifested as a catastrophic shift in the ambient reality around him. The very air grew cold and brittle, the light turning sickly and sharp.
It was the expression of a being who had been the absolute center of all mathematical certainty for eons, suddenly realizing he was nothing more than an error in someone else’s equation.

Desperation flickered in his eyes, and Kaeleth reached for a working. His fingers twitched, beginning to weave the first threads of a temporal severance, a spell that would have unmade Rex’s past to erase his present.
Rex didn’t give him the chance.
"Too slow," Rex growled.

Rex slammed his fist into the air, unleashing Gravity Manipulation at maximum local concentration. He didn’t just increase the weight; he created a localized singularity directly in front of Kaeleth’s hands.

The spell was interrupted mid-formation. In the divine calculus, an interrupted working is worse than a failed one; it becomes a mass of raw, unchanneled potential that refuses to return to its source.
It becomes a bomb.
The discharge exploded outward in a sphere of crushing force and temporal feedback. The sound was not an explosion but a wet, tearing shriek as space itself screamed under the pressure.
The force caught Kaeleth’s center mass. His divine form buckled as the gravity tore at his molecular coherence, sending him hurtling backward like a broken marionette.
He slammed into the domain’s far wall with enough force to shatter stone, the impact producing a sickening crunch as his divine ribs made of solidified light and authority fractured under the trauma.

Kaeleth slid down the wall, coughing up globs of luminous gold blood. His form flickered erratically, his divine coherence struggling to stitch itself back together while his consciousness fought to process the simultaneous trauma of the wall impact and the gravitational discharge.
He was drowning in sensation, his mind a storm of pain and disorientation.
Rex didn’t wait for him to recover. He was already moving.
Rex sprinted toward the throne. The throne wasn’t just furniture; it was the heartbeat of this reality.
It was the domain’s primary architectural structure, the physical manifestation of Kaeleth’s very identity.
It was the anchor around which every law of physics in this space had been spun. To destroy the throne was to lobotomize the domain.
Rex reached it in seconds, his shadow stretching long and menacing across the throne’s surface.
"This ends now," Rex whispered, his eyes burning with the fire of the Forbidden God.

He channeled the Earthen Authority, but he didn’t approach it as a simple geologist. He infused the command with the terrifying molecular precision granted by his Full Potential Telekinesisfull potential telekinesis.
He wasn’t just trying to break stone; he was targeting the fundamental bonds holding the divine substance together.
The throne’s material was alien amber gold temporal notation solidified into a physical form. It was harder than diamond and more complex than any alloy known to man.
But Rex’s power didn’t care about hardness. It cared about structure.
Rex found the seams. He found the microscopic lines where the temporal notation had been fused during the throne’s creation—the spiritual welds that held the god’s authority in place.
Crack.
A sound like a lightning strike echoed through the sanctum. The throne didn’t break like rock; it splintered along those divine seams, the golden light bleeding out of the cracks like molten marrow.
Rex slammed both palms against the surface, his muscles bulging, tendons standing out like cables as he poured every ounce of his devastating will into the structure.
"BREAK!" Rex roared.
With a sound that mimicked the breaking of a world, the throne shattered.
The collapse of the anchor structure triggered an immediate, violent reaction. The domain’s ambient medium went berserk.

The amber gold symbols that had been flowing in graceful, predictable patterns suddenly turned into a maelstrom of chaotic energy. The very air became a turbulent vortex of fractured time, shredding anything caught in its path.
The reference point was gone.
The logic of the space had died.
The floor buckled and heaved like the deck of a ship in a hurricane. The shockwave of the throne’s destruction tore through the ground, sending debris flying like shrapnel.
In the center of the chaos, stripped of his anchor, stripped of his authority, and stripped of his dignity, Kaeleth collapsed.
The god fell to his knees, his form flickering weakly as the world he had built around himself tore itself apart.

"Seventeen coverage extensions where I had to remap my own existence to survive you."
Rex took a step forward.
The floor beneath his boot groaned as if protesting his approach.

"And at the end of that seventeenth strike, that last pathetic attempt to fracture my soul, the Adaptation’s analysis speed for temporal class workings was running at approximately forty percent of the initial baseline."
"I’m not learning in increments anymore, Kaeleth..."
"I’m learning in leaps...
I’m learning faster than you can think."
Rex began walking toward him.
It wasn’t a charge; it was a slow, inexorable march.’
The kind of walk a butcher takes toward a stunned animal.
"You ran out of new things, didn’t you?" Rex’s voice grew darker, more predatory.
"The temporal domain’s working set is finite."
"You have a god’s arsenal... you have countless expressions of temporal authority."
"You can slow time, you can loop it, you can fracture it into shards.
But they are all just different faces on the same coin."
"They all share one fundamental mechanism."
Rex was ten meters away now.
He could see the way Kaeleth’s divine armor was hairline fractured, the way the golden light flickered like a dying candle in a hurricane.

"Once the Adaptation has covered that fundamental mechanism through enough implementations, the coverage extends to the general case," Rex explained, his inner monologue a cold stream of tactical certainty. ’He’s cornered.’
He’s a king with no kingdom left, a scholar with no words left.’
’Now, I break what’s left.’
"It doesn’t matter which flavor of time you throw at me...
I’ve already learned the recipe."
The distance closed.
Nine meters.
Eight.
"You cannot produce a new mechanism," Rex said, his voice dropping to a guttural whisper that seemed to vibrate in Kaeleth’s very bones.
"You’ve been practicing the same divine arts for two thousand years."
"You’re a master of your domain, yes.
But mastery isn’t invention."
"You cannot invent a new class of working on demand, because working classes aren’t things you do."
"They are properties of the domain itself.
And your domain?
Your domain is exhausted."
Rex stopped five meters away.
He stood there, a mountain of scarred muscle and murderous intent, looming over the broken deity.
The air between them crackled with the static of Rex’s unleashed power, a physical pressure that made the very air scream.
Rex’s eyes locked onto Kaeleth’s, no mercy, no hesitation, only the cold satisfaction of a predator who has already won.
"You’re out of options," Rex said.
Kaeleth raised his gaze.
There was something profoundly wrong with the way he looked at Rex.
When a mortal runs out of options, they collapse into a predictable biological cascade: sweat, dilated pupils, the frantic heaving of lungs, and the primal stench of terror.
But a god?
A god’s desperation was something far more alien.
Kaeleth’s defeat didn’t manifest as fear; it manifested as a catastrophic shift in the ambient reality around him.
The very air grew cold and brittle, the light turning sickly and sharp.
It was the expression of a being who had been the absolute center of all mathematical certainty for eons, suddenly realizing he was nothing more than an error in someone else’s equation.
Desperation flickered in his eyes, and Kaeleth reached for a working.
His fingers twitched, beginning to weave the first threads of a temporal severance, a spell that would have unmade Rex’s past to erase his present.
Rex didn’t give him the chance.
"Too slow," Rex growled.
Rex slammed his fist into the air, unleashing Gravity Manipulation at maximum local concentration.
He didn’t just increase the weight; he created a localized singularity directly in front of Kaeleth’s hands.
The spell was interrupted mid-formation.
In the divine calculus, an interrupted working is worse than a failed one; it becomes a mass of raw, unchanneled potential that refuses to return to its source.
It becomes a bomb.
The discharge exploded outward in a sphere of crushing force and temporal feedback.
The sound was not an explosion but a wet, tearing shriek as space itself screamed under the pressure.
The force caught Kaeleth’s center mass.
His divine form buckled as the gravity tore at his molecular coherence, sending him hurtling backward like a broken marionette.
He slammed into the domain’s far wall with enough force to shatter stone, the impact producing a sickening crunch as his divine ribs made of solidified light and authority fractured under the trauma.
Kaeleth slid down the wall, coughing up globs of luminous gold blood.

His form flickered erratically, his divine coherence struggling to stitch itself back together while his consciousness fought to process the simultaneous trauma of the wall impact and the gravitational discharge.
He was drowning in sensation, his mind a storm of pain and disorientation.
Rex didn’t wait for him to recover.
He was already moving.
Rex sprinted toward the throne.
The throne wasn’t just furniture; it was the heartbeat of this reality.
It was the domain’s primary architectural structure, the physical manifestation of Kaeleth’s very identity.
It was the anchor around which every law of physics in this space had been spun.
To destroy the throne was to lobotomize the domain.
Rex reached it in seconds, his shadow stretching long and menacing across the throne’s surface.
"This ends now," Rex whispered, his eyes burning with the fire of the Forbidden God.
He channeled the Earthen Authority, but he didn’t approach it as a simple geologist.
He infused the command with the terrifying molecular precision granted by his Full Potential Telekinesisfull potential telekinesis.
He wasn’t just trying to break stone; he was targeting the fundamental bonds holding the divine substance together.
The throne’s material was alien amber gold temporal notation solidified into a physical form.
It was harder than diamond and more complex than any alloy known to man.
But Rex’s power didn’t care about hardness.
It cared about structure.
Rex found the seams.
He found the microscopic lines where the temporal notation had been fused during the throne’s creation—the spiritual welds that held the god’s authority in place.
Crack.
A sound like a lightning strike echoed through the sanctum.
The throne didn’t break like rock; it splintered along those divine seams, the golden light bleeding out of the cracks like molten marrow.
Rex slammed both palms against the surface, his muscles bulging, tendons standing out like cables as he poured every ounce of his devastating will into the structure.
"BREAK!" Rex roared.
With a sound that mimicked the breaking of a world, the throne shattered.
The collapse of the anchor structure triggered an immediate, violent reaction.
The domain’s ambient medium went berserk.
The amber gold symbols that had been flowing in graceful, predictable patterns suddenly turned into a maelstrom of chaotic energy.
The very air became a turbulent vortex of fractured time, shredding anything caught in its path.
The reference point was gone.
The logic of the space had died.
The floor buckled and heaved like the deck of a ship in a hurricane.
The shockwave of the throne’s destruction tore through the ground, sending debris flying like shrapnel.
In the center of the chaos, stripped of his anchor, stripped of his authority, and stripped of his dignity, Kaeleth collapsed.
The god fell to his knees, his form flickering weakly as the world he had built around himself tore itself apart.

chapters.title: Chapter 1076. A Supernova Contained in the Shape of a Man
paragraphs: Rex moved through the chaos with the terrifying, unhurried gait of a reaper approaching a harvest already completed. The domain around him was a nightmare of fractured reality; the floor buckled like wounded flesh, and the amber gold air screamed as it tore apart without its anchor.

Shards of the divine throne and crystallized time whipped through the air like shrapnel, but Rex walked through the storm as if it were nothing more than a light breeze. His boots crunched on debris that used to be the foundation of a god’s power.
Kaeleth lay broken on the heaving floor. Without the throne, his divine coherence was hemorrhaging.
His form flickered like a dying hologram, translucent patches of his body revealing the raw, bleeding void beneath.

Every time his essence tried to reassert itself, the chaotic domain rejected it, sending fresh waves of agony through his nerves. He looked less like a god and more like a corpse made of fading light.
Rex reached him and crouched, bringing himself level with the fallen deity. The proximity was intimate, almost tender in its brutality.
"The throne," Rex said, his voice cutting through the howling temporal winds with chilling clarity. "Your anchor."
"The singular point around which your two thousand-year reign has spiraled."
"The lynchpin that held every law, every moment, and every breath of this domain together."
"It is gone, Kaeleth... You are untethered."
Rex leaned closer, studying the way Kaeleth’s essence leaked onto the cracked floor in shimmering, viscous pools of gold.
"I’ve dissected your little gambit," Rex continued, his eyes cold and analytical. "Your plan was elegant in its cruelty."
"You sought to manufacture a mortal vessel, a puppet forged from trauma, and point it at me."
"You banked on the idea that the vessel’s personal history with me would grant it the intimate access a stranger could never achieve."
"You wanted the vessel’s designation to carry enough borrowed authority to bypass my defenses."
"And if the puppet broke? Well, puppets are expendable."
Rex paused, letting the silence of the dying domain underscore his words. He watched a spark of gold blood bubble at Kaeleth’s lips.
"Your plan suffered two catastrophic failures," Rex said. "The first was your failure to understand the human variable."
"The vessel chose to surrender its designation rather than remain your weapon."
"That wasn’t a flaw in your mathematics, Kaeleth; it was a flaw in your selection."
"You thought Theo Morr Nightwing was a man stripped of everything."
"But there is a difference between having no attachments and being convinced you have none. When his mother appeared, the illusion shattered."
"The weapon became a man again."
Rex’s expression shifted to a slow, predatory smile that didn’t reach his eyes.
"The second failure," Rex whispered, "was me."
"But I think you’ve been feeling that failure in your bones for the last hour."
Kaeleth’s breathing was wet and labored. He lifted his head, his eyes glassy with pain and the dawning horror of his situation.
Even as a broken thing, his voice carried the fading echo of command.
"You are going to take it," Kaeleth rasped, each word costing him a fresh spasm of agony. "You’re going to take the authority."
"Yes," Rex answered simply.
"The temporal authority over Aethelgard," Kaeleth said, his voice cracking. "Not the general domain."
"Don’t be arrogant, mortal."
"You cannot absorb the general temporal domain... Its scale exceeds your current capacity, and it would incinerate your soul before you could grasp it."
Rex didn’t flinch. "I know what I can handle."
"I’m not reaching for the ocean, Kaeleth... I’m not trying to swallow the general domain."
Rex’s eyes burned with a focused, terrifying hunger. "I am taking the operational component."
"The specific, concentrated expression of temporal authority that you have been bleeding into Aethelgard’s foundational layer for two millennia."
"The part you actually use."
Kaeleth’s jaw tightened. "And with it..."
"Control over the temporal substrate of this specific location," Rex finished for him. "I won’t own time itself."
"But I will own the time that happens here."
"I will own every second that passes within these borders... I will own you."
Kaeleth fell silent. The only sound was the grinding of the collapsing domain and the wet, fading heartbeat of a god who had finally run out of miracles.
"Many things I do have not existed before," Rex said, his voice a low rumble that seemed to vibrate through the very marrow of the crumbling reality. "And the thing that exists now is your end."
For a heartbeat, there was only the sound of the dying domain, the wet dripping of divine ichor, and the distant crackle of fractured time. Then, the atmosphere changed.
Kaeleth’s compressed, broken form did not merely heal; it underwent a violent metamorphosis. This was not the measured recovery of a warrior stitching wounds or a mortal catching their breath.
This was something far more terrifying. It was the instantaneous decision of a cornered apex predator that had decided to stop playing with its prey and begin its slaughter.

It was the choice of a god who realized that half measures had already cost him his throne and that survival now demanded he become everything—every law, every force, every nightmare—all at once, or die in the attempt.
Rex felt it first through his Divine Perception. The sensation was like a sudden, crushing pressure behind his eyes—the unmistakable feeling of an entity abandoning all restraint.
For two thousand years, Kaeleth had ruled with the careful hand of an administrator, holding back the true tide of his power because he had never needed to see what lay beneath the surface.
But now, with the throne shattered and his authority bleeding out, there was no more reason to be gentle. There was no longer any posture to protect.
The domain’s ambient medium, which had been swirling in a chaotic, mindless maelstrom since the throne’s destruction, suddenly froze.
The turbulence didn’t dissipate; it obeyed.

Every shard of fractured time, every floating piece of amber gold debris, and every scream of displaced energy ceased its random flight. They stopped midair, suspended in a terrifying stillness, before snapping into alignment.
The chaos didn’t vanish; it reorganized itself. The entire reality of Aethelgard suddenly pivoted on a new axis, and that axis was Kaeleth.
Rex’s inner mind raced, his thoughts a frantic calculation of power scales.
’He’s not trying to rebuild his throne,’ Rex realized, his teeth grinding together as the air began to hum with lethal frequency. ’He’s turning himself into the throne.’
A sound began to rise from the floor, a low-frequency growl that wasn’t sound so much as it was the universe protesting a violation of its fundamental laws.
Kaeleth’s blood, that luminous gold ichor, began to boil. It didn’t drip; it levitated, spiraling upward around his body in angry, molten ribbons.
The wounds in his divine form didn’t just close; they fused with searing heat, cauterizing his essence with raw power that smelled of burnt ozone and ancient copper.
A shockwave of pure, unfiltered rage erupted from Kaeleth’s center. It hit Rex like a physical blow, forcing him to plant his feet as the ground beneath him spiderwebbed from the sheer pressure.

The light in the room shifted from amber gold to a blinding, apocalyptic white. The temperature skyrocketed, then plummeted to absolute zero in the span of a second, each fluctuation threatening to tear Rex’s molecular structure apart.

Kaeleth wasn’t just angry; he was a supernova contained within the shape of a man. His eyes weren’t eyes anymore; they were twin voids of temporal fury, seeing every possible moment of Rex’s death simultaneously.
The pressure became unbearable. Bones creaked audibly in Rex’s body as the gravity around Kaeleth intensified to impossible levels.
The divine ichor spiraling around him hardened into jagged, razor-sharp armor of solidified time, each spike humming with enough energy to cleave through dimensions.

Through the blinding glare and the deafening shriek of reality bending to his will, Kaeleth rose. He didn’t climb to his feet; he ascended, his body unfolding with a terrifying, unnatural grace as he reclaimed his height.
He stood tall, silhouetted against the collapsing sky of his own domain, no longer a wounded king, but a vengeful god made flesh.

chapters.title: Chapter 1077. What I Have Shown You vs What I Am
paragraphs: The amber gold radiance that had been flickering like a dying candle since the throne’s destruction suddenly exploded. It wasn’t just light; it was a supernova of temporal energy that roared back to life with a brightness that exceeded anything Rex had registered throughout the entire engagement.

The temporal notation—the raw script of reality—began to bleed through the air, the walls, and the shattered floor at such a terrifying density that the domain appeared to be ablaze with something far more lethal than fire. It was a conflagration of pure causality.
Kaeleth’s form began to change. He didn’t grow in physical height or mass, but his presence underwent a grotesque expansion.
He began to occupy more of the ambient register, his very existence stretching to fill every crack and crevice of Aethelgard. He had stopped pretending.
The mask of the administrator was gone; the predator had filled the cage.
"You think you understand the mathematics," Kaeleth’s voice boomed.
It no longer came from a single throat; it resonated from the walls, the floor, and the air itself. The domain was no longer his battlefield; the domain was Kaeleth.
"You think seventeen mechanisms constitute the complete set?"
"You think you have mapped the limits of my design?"
Rex didn’t answer. His mind was screaming warnings.

His martial arts mastery wasn’t just analyzing a stance; it was screaming a primal alarm, translating the shift in Kaeleth’s divine posture into a single, terrifying truth: ’Distance has become irrelevant.’ Survival probability is plummeting.’
’Move. Now. ’Rex’s inner voice was a blade of focus cutting through the chaos. ’He’s not attacking me.’
’He’s attacking the space I occupy.’
"There is a difference," Kaeleth roared as the reality around them began to warp and scream, "between what I have shown you... and what I AM."
The first worker arrived before Rex could even complete his repositioning.
It wasn’t a spell. It wasn’t a strike. It was a catastrophic collapse.
The entire temporal fabric of the domain imploded toward Kaeleth’s position with the force of a collapsing star, only to rebound outward in a single, violent pulse of absolute annihilation.
Kaeleth was using the domain as a limb, swinging the very concept of ’now’ like a sledgehammer.
This wasn’t a single mechanism. The adaptation couldn’t categorize it.

It was a compound catastrophe: acceleration, deceleration, severance, and fracture all compressed into one impossible moment. Kaeleth had stopped bothering to distinguish between his powers; he was simply unleashing the raw fury of time itself.
Rex took the hit head-on. There was no escape.
When the ground you stand on becomes the weapon, there is no cover.

The adaptation stuttered. Faced with a simultaneous assault of contradictory mechanisms, the system spent two agonizing seconds trying to parse the data, trying to understand how to file a phenomenon that was simultaneously speeding up and slowing down, breaking and mending.
In the calculus of god-tier combat, two seconds was an eternity. Two seconds was long enough to die.
The pulse tore through Rex’s biological timeline with the brutality of a meat grinder. Rex screamed as he felt his own history being shredded.
In a single heartbeat, his hands aged decades, the skin wrinkling and spotting with liver marks, only to reverse in a wet, nauseating stutter back to youth, then age again.

His bones groaned as they calcified and softened in rapid succession. The Infinite Regeneration fought desperately to smooth out the damage, but it was trying to repair a foundation that was constantly shifting.
Underneath the physical agony, a deeper horror took root: a fracture in his consciousness. His sense of continuity shattered.
For a moment, Rex couldn’t remember if he had already been hit, if he was currently being hit, or if he had already died.
The ’now’ became a kaleidoscope of broken moments.
The force of the pulse launched Rex across the domain like a ragdoll. He struck the far wall with a sound like a sledgehammer hitting wet concrete.
The amber gold surface cracked behind him as his body embedded itself into the debris, ribs snapping with audible, wet cracks that echoed through the chamber.
Blood bright, arterial red sprayed across the golden floor, steaming as it touched the charged air.
Rex coughed, tasting copper and something ancient, his vision swimming in a haze of temporal static. His lungs burned, each breath a struggle against the reality that seemed to reject his presence.
But Kaeleth was not finished. The god was not giving him a moment to breathe, let alone to heal.
The golden storm began to gather again, more focused now, more murderous. The hunt had truly begun.
Kaeleth didn’t run; he simply ceased to be in one position and appeared in another, crossing the distance with a speed that shattered the sound barrier before the shockwave could even form.

The blade that coalesced from his robes this time was no longer a weapon; it was a nightmare. A dozen shards of solidified temporal notation orbited his hand like a constellation of razor-sharp stars, each fragment lashing out independently with its own unique severance property.
They moved with a hive mind intelligence, seeking every weakness, every gap in Rex’s guard.
Rex’s reflexes screamed. He threw his forearm up just as the first three shards shrieked through the air.

The impact felt like being struck by lightning; the vibration rattled his teeth and threatened to split his radius. But the fourth shard was faster. It found the gap between his guard and his shoulder, slicing through flesh and bone alike.
Rex didn’t just bleed. The wound screamed with a metaphysical agony.
Instead of crimson blood, the gash leaked moments.

Through the torn muscle and severed artery, Rex could see a visible thinning in reality, glimmering fragments of his own past and future being pulled loose from his body like loose threads from a tapestry, scattering into the air as useless shrapnel of time.
’Focus, dammit!’ Rex’s inner voice roared over the ringing in his ears. ’Don’t think about the wound.’
’Don’t think about the seconds you’re losing.’
’If you hesitate, you’re already dead.’

Instead of retreating into the safety of distance, Rex made a desperate, suicidal calculation: he shoved off the cracked wall, muscles straining against the crushing gravity, and charged directly into the storm.
He knew that retreating would only give Kaeleth the space to continue weaving these devastating compound workings. He had to force this into a brawl.
He had to make it personal.
Kaeleth met him head-on with the fury of a collapsing star.
The fight devolved from a tactical engagement into a primal collision of two unstoppable forces. There was no more finesse, no more measured exchanges.

It was raw, ugly, and devastating. Kaeleth threw everything the domain could conjure: shards of frozen time and waves of accelerated entropy, while Rex absorbed the worst of it, his body becoming a canvas of violence.
The god’s blades became a blur of lethal light. Rex felt the sting of a dozen shallow cuts across his chest and arms. Each one was a theft; each cut stole a fragment of his continuity.
His Infinite Regeneration worked overtime, knitting flesh together as fast as it was torn, but it couldn’t fix the fraying of his soul.
Rex felt a nauseating unsteadiness creeping into his perception; he would swing a fist, only to feel as though he had already swung it three seconds ago or was yet to swing it at all.
’The clock is ticking,’ Rex thought grimly, his mind fighting through the temporal static. ’ My regeneration can fix my bones, but it can’t fix my timeline.’
’If I lose too many seconds, there won’t be enough of me left to regenerate.’
He drove forward anyway, fueled by pure, stubborn defiance.

His earthly authority answered his desperate intent before his conscious mind could even formulate the command. With a guttural roar, he ripped a massive slab of the amber gold floor free, hurling it like a shield into the path of the orbiting blades.
The collision was thunderous stone grinding against temporal energy in a shower of sparks and debris.
That half second of interrupted rhythm was all he needed.

Rex closed the final distance, his boots skidding on blood-slicked stone. He channeled every ounce of his gravity manipulation and telekinesis into his right fist, condensing the weight of a mountain into a single point of impact.
He drove the strike straight into Kaeleth’s chest.
CRACK.
The sound of the impact reverberated through the entire domain. Kaeleth staggered backward, his divine form convulsing as the concentrated force of the blow bypassed his temporal defenses.
It was the first time since Kaeleth had unleashed his full power that he had actually given ground. Rex saw it immediately: the stagger wasn’t just physical; it was systemic.
Kaeleth was burning through his divine reserves at a catastrophic rate. By choosing to unleash everything at once, the god had abandoned the economy of power.
He was trading his eternal essence for immediate, overwhelming destruction.
Rex stood his ground, breathing hard, blood dripping from his chin as his own temporal wounds continued to leak seconds into the air. His voice came out rough, cracked like broken glass.

"You’re spending yourself," Rex rasped, each word a battle against the disorientation clawing at his brain. "Every mechanism you throw at once instead of one at a time is a mechanism you can’t use again for a long time."
"You know the math, Kaeleth. You’re burning your own foundation to kill me."

sentences.text: The amber gold radiance that had been flickering like a dying candle since the throne’s destruction suddenly exploded.
It wasn’t just light; it was a supernova of temporal energy that roared back to life with a brightness that exceeded anything Rex had registered throughout the entire engagement.

The temporal notation—the raw script of reality—began to bleed through the air, the walls, and the shattered floor at such a terrifying density that the domain appeared to be ablaze with something far more lethal than fire.
It was a conflagration of pure causality.
Kaeleth’s form began to change.
He didn’t grow in physical height or mass, but his presence underwent a grotesque expansion.
He began to occupy more of the ambient register, his very existence stretching to fill every crack and crevice of Aethelgard.
He had stopped pretending.
The mask of the administrator was gone; the predator had filled the cage.
"You think you understand the mathematics," Kaeleth’s voice boomed.
It no longer came from a single throat; it resonated from the walls, the floor, and the air itself.
The domain was no longer his battlefield; the domain was Kaeleth.
"You think seventeen mechanisms constitute the complete set?"
"You think you have mapped the limits of my design?"
Rex didn’t answer.
His mind was screaming warnings.

His martial arts mastery wasn’t just analyzing a stance; it was screaming a primal alarm, translating the shift in Kaeleth’s divine posture into a single, terrifying truth: ’Distance has become irrelevant.’ Survival probability is plummeting.’
’Move.
Now. ’Rex’s inner voice was a blade of focus cutting through the chaos. ’He’s not attacking me.’
’He’s attacking the space I occupy.’
"There is a difference," Kaeleth roared as the reality around them began to warp and scream, "between what I have shown you... and what I AM."
The first worker arrived before Rex could even complete his repositioning.
It wasn’t a spell.
It wasn’t a strike.
It was a catastrophic collapse.
The entire temporal fabric of the domain imploded toward Kaeleth’s position with the force of a collapsing star, only to rebound outward in a single, violent pulse of absolute annihilation.
Kaeleth was using the domain as a limb, swinging the very concept of ’now’ like a sledgehammer.
This wasn’t a single mechanism.
The adaptation couldn’t categorize it.
It was a compound catastrophe: acceleration, deceleration, severance, and fracture all compressed into one impossible moment.
Kaeleth had stopped bothering to distinguish between his powers; he was simply unleashing the raw fury of time itself.
Rex took the hit head-on.
There was no escape.
When the ground you stand on becomes the weapon, there is no cover.
The adaptation stuttered.

Faced with a simultaneous assault of contradictory mechanisms, the system spent two agonizing seconds trying to parse the data, trying to understand how to file a phenomenon that was simultaneously speeding up and slowing down, breaking and mending.
In the calculus of god-tier combat, two seconds was an eternity.
Two seconds was long enough to die.
The pulse tore through Rex’s biological timeline with the brutality of a meat grinder.
Rex screamed as he felt his own history being shredded.
In a single heartbeat, his hands aged decades, the skin wrinkling and spotting with liver marks, only to reverse in a wet, nauseating stutter back to youth, then age again.
His bones groaned as they calcified and softened in rapid succession.
The Infinite Regeneration fought desperately to smooth out the damage, but it was trying to repair a foundation that was constantly shifting.
Underneath the physical agony, a deeper horror took root: a fracture in his consciousness.
His sense of continuity shattered.
For a moment, Rex couldn’t remember if he had already been hit, if he was currently being hit, or if he had already died.
The ’now’ became a kaleidoscope of broken moments.
The force of the pulse launched Rex across the domain like a ragdoll.
He struck the far wall with a sound like a sledgehammer hitting wet concrete.
The amber gold surface cracked behind him as his body embedded itself into the debris, ribs snapping with audible, wet cracks that echoed through the chamber.
Blood bright, arterial red sprayed across the golden floor, steaming as it touched the charged air.
Rex coughed, tasting copper and something ancient, his vision swimming in a haze of temporal static.
His lungs burned, each breath a struggle against the reality that seemed to reject his presence.
But Kaeleth was not finished.
The god was not giving him a moment to breathe, let alone to heal.
The golden storm began to gather again, more focused now, more murderous.
The hunt had truly begun.
Kaeleth didn’t run; he simply ceased to be in one position and appeared in another, crossing the distance with a speed that shattered the sound barrier before the shockwave could even form.
The blade that coalesced from his robes this time was no longer a weapon; it was a nightmare.
A dozen shards of solidified temporal notation orbited his hand like a constellation of razor-sharp stars, each fragment lashing out independently with its own unique severance property.
They moved with a hive mind intelligence, seeking every weakness, every gap in Rex’s guard.
Rex’s reflexes screamed.
He threw his forearm up just as the first three shards shrieked through the air.
The impact felt like being struck by lightning; the vibration rattled his teeth and threatened to split his radius.
But the fourth shard was faster.
It found the gap between his guard and his shoulder, slicing through flesh and bone alike.
Rex didn’t just bleed.
The wound screamed with a metaphysical agony.
Instead of crimson blood, the gash leaked moments.

Through the torn muscle and severed artery, Rex could see a visible thinning in reality, glimmering fragments of his own past and future being pulled loose from his body like loose threads from a tapestry, scattering into the air as useless shrapnel of time.
’Focus, dammit!’ Rex’s inner voice roared over the ringing in his ears. ’Don’t think about the wound.’
’Don’t think about the seconds you’re losing.’
’If you hesitate, you’re already dead.’

Instead of retreating into the safety of distance, Rex made a desperate, suicidal calculation: he shoved off the cracked wall, muscles straining against the crushing gravity, and charged directly into the storm.
He knew that retreating would only give Kaeleth the space to continue weaving these devastating compound workings.
He had to force this into a brawl.
He had to make it personal.
Kaeleth met him head-on with the fury of a collapsing star.
The fight devolved from a tactical engagement into a primal collision of two unstoppable forces.
There was no more finesse, no more measured exchanges.
It was raw, ugly, and devastating.
Kaeleth threw everything the domain could conjure: shards of frozen time and waves of accelerated entropy, while Rex absorbed the worst of it, his body becoming a canvas of violence.
The god’s blades became a blur of lethal light.
Rex felt the sting of a dozen shallow cuts across his chest and arms.
Each one was a theft; each cut stole a fragment of his continuity.
His Infinite Regeneration worked overtime, knitting flesh together as fast as it was torn, but it couldn’t fix the fraying of his soul.
Rex felt a nauseating unsteadiness creeping into his perception; he would swing a fist, only to feel as though he had already swung it three seconds ago or was yet to swing it at all.
’The clock is ticking,’ Rex thought grimly, his mind fighting through the temporal static. ’ My regeneration can fix my bones, but it can’t fix my timeline.’
’If I lose too many seconds, there won’t be enough of me left to regenerate.’
He drove forward anyway, fueled by pure, stubborn defiance.
His earthly authority answered his desperate intent before his conscious mind could even formulate the command.
With a guttural roar, he ripped a massive slab of the amber gold floor free, hurling it like a shield into the path of the orbiting blades.
The collision was thunderous stone grinding against temporal energy in a shower of sparks and debris.
That half second of interrupted rhythm was all he needed.
Rex closed the final distance, his boots skidding on blood-slicked stone.
He channeled every ounce of his gravity manipulation and telekinesis into his right fist, condensing the weight of a mountain into a single point of impact.
He drove the strike straight into Kaeleth’s chest.
CRACK.
The sound of the impact reverberated through the entire domain.
Kaeleth staggered backward, his divine form convulsing as the concentrated force of the blow bypassed his temporal defenses.
It was the first time since Kaeleth had unleashed his full power that he had actually given ground.
Rex saw it immediately: the stagger wasn’t just physical; it was systemic.
Kaeleth was burning through his divine reserves at a catastrophic rate.
By choosing to unleash everything at once, the god had abandoned the economy of power.
He was trading his eternal essence for immediate, overwhelming destruction.
